<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comTue, 10 Nov 2026 19:19:51 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[European shares near record high as lower oil prices boost sentiment]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/european-shares-near-record-high-as-lower-oil-prices-boost-sentiment/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/european-shares-near-record-high-as-lower-oil-prices-boost-sentiment/Tue, 10 Nov 2026 18:04:02 +0000European shares edged higher on Tuesday, hovering near a record high as falling oil prices and easing ​concerns over a possible military escalation between the US-Israeli coalition and Iran boosted risk appetite.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 index gained 0.3 per cent to 658.32, within two points of an all-time highest close, reached in August.

DUBLIN

The Iseq All-Share index rose 1 per cent to 15,025.86.

Kingspan rose 1.3 per cent to €96.70 as the group outlined ambitious financial targets out to 2030, including a goal to more than double trading profits to €2 billion.

Banking stocks were among the main gainers, tracking the performance of the broader sector across Europe. AIB and Bank of Ireland jumped 1.9 per cent to €11.58 and €19.60, respectively, as European Central Bank chief economist Philip Lane said it would be prudent for the institution to raise official interest rates again in December.

Housebuilders, however, were out of sorts, with Cairn Homes falling 0.5 per cent to €2.78 and Glenveagh Properties dropping 1.4 per cent to €2.41.

Ryanair edged 0.7 per cent higher to €26.61 amid easing oil prices.

Irish Continental Group was also in focus as the High Court approved its €8-a-share takeover by management led by chief executive Eamonn Rothwell. It dipped 0.3 per cent to €7.96.

LONDON

The FTSE 100 has closed 0.3 per cent lower in London as early advances evaporated in the wake of another strong US inflation print.

Oil majors BP and Shell fell 0.8 per cent and 2.1 per cent, respectively, as oil prices dipped.

The strong dollar put pressure on the price of gold, sending miners Fresnillo and Endeavour Mining down 4.7 per cent and 4.3 per cent, respectively.

Marks & Spencer was a prominent gainer, up 4.1 per cent, as it outlined the next phase of its transformation strategy at a capital markets day event.

On the FTSE 250, Funding Circle leapt 13 per cent as it upgraded its full-year expectations, citing resilient demand from small and medium-sized enterprises.

EUROPE

⁠Lufthansa rose 1.3 per cent and Air ​France-KLM soared 3.4 per cent as sector followers monitored oil prices.

Infineon added 0.9 per cent after the German chipmaker forecast revenue growth of more than 20 per cent in 2027 and a roughly five-percentage-point increase in ‌profitability.

French payment services firm Edenred rose 6.4 per cent after a Brazilian judge suspended part of new meal voucher ‌rules for companies in a local lobby group, including Pluxee and Edenred’s Ticket.

NEW YORK

Wall Street’s main indexes were in retreat in early afternoon trading, pausing a ‌two-day rebound in tech shares, after a hotter-than-expected October inflation reading reinforced fears that the Federal Reserve could keep interest rates higher for longer.

Earlier in the day, Fed ​governor Christopher Waller said the central bank should raise interest rates by at least a quarter of a percentage point next month even if inflation cooled in October. If price pressures accelerated, policymakers should consider a half-percentage-point increase, he said.

Among rate-sensitive ⁠sectors, financials rose, while utilities and real estate were ​among the laggards.

Shares of Nvidia, the second-most valuable company in the world, fell. Chief executive Jensen Huang’s affair with Chinese businesswoman ‌Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for Beijing, ​facilitated the shipment of at least $7.5 billion (€6.7 billion) worth of the company’s chips through Chinese firms, The Information reported.

As chief executive of the company ⁠at the heart of the AI boom, Huang’s leadership ⁠and future at Nvidia are ​crucial to investors.

Attention is also turning to Anthropic’s expected public listing later this month. The AI lab revealed that its initial public offering is expected to raise as much as $64.4 billion, giving the company a fully diluted valuation of up to $1.4 trillion.

Media giant Skydance dropped after it announced cost-cutting plans and warned that the underperformance of Warner Brothers’ film slate would impact ‌fourth-quarter profit by up to $200 million.

Still, cooling oil prices offered some comfort, with Brent crude futures slipping below $90 a barrel for the first time since August. – Additional reporting: Reuters/PA

]]><![CDATA[Cork solicitor due to retire this week prohibited from practising by High Court]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/cork-solicitor-due-to-retire-this-week-prohibited-from-practice-by-high-court/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/cork-solicitor-due-to-retire-this-week-prohibited-from-practice-by-high-court/Tue, 10 Nov 2026 17:22:55 +0000A Cork solicitor has been prohibited by the High Court from practising even though he has indicated to the Law Society he is going to retire this week and close his office.

The Legal Services Regulatory Authority (LSRA) sought an order from the court that John Moylan, of Richard Moylan & Co Solicitors, Shortcastle Street, Mallow, Co Cork, be censured and prohibited from practising as a legal practitioner otherwise than as an employee.

This came after the Legal Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal last year made two findings of misconduct against Moylan.

This followed an inquiry into allegations that the solicitor had failed to take any adequate steps to register an enduring power of attorney for an elderly man in a nursing home or to reply adequately or at all to correspondence or phone calls from a member of the man’s family.

In an affidavit to the court, Antony Watson, LSRA head of complaints, investigations and resolutions, said the tribunal considered the sanction necessary to protect the public, maintain the reputation of the solicitors’ profession, to punish Moylan and to discourage him and other members of the profession from repeating or emulating the misconduct.

High Court president Judge David Barniville said he was satisfied that the sanction was appropriate and proportionate.

Moylan will also have to pay €1,500 as restitution to the woman who had complained that the solicitor had failed to register an enduring power of attorney for her grandfather.

Moylan (72), who has been a solicitor for 48 years, has indicated he is to retire on Friday this week and was liaising with the Law Society in relation to a wind-down of his practice, the court heard.

Earlier, during a separate application by the Law Society, the judge was told that Moylan had indicated he intended to retire from the practice this week, but the Law Society needed an order from the court so it could take control of the solicitor’s practice and facilitate an orderly wind-down.

Moylan was consenting to the orders sought. The judge said he was satisfied the orders sought were appropriate.

On the LSRA matter before the court, Watson in his affidavit said the tribunal held an inquiry into two allegations in relation to the complaint.

Watson said Moylan indicated that he admitted the facts. He had been instructed by a man in the summer of 2020 to prepare an enduring power of attorney. It was to be registered when the man lost capacity. Moylan was informed in July 2022 that the man had lost capacity and the solicitor was asked by his granddaughter to register the enduring power of attorney.

Moylan failed to reply adequately or at all to correspondence from the man’s granddaughter or to return her calls and emails sent between August 2022 and December 2022, it was claimed.

The woman gave evidence to the inquiry about her grandfather’s declining health and the need to discharge his nursing home bills.

Watson said the tribunal found the allegations were proven as to fact and “proven as to misconduct being an act or omission connected with the provision by the solicitor of legal services which were to a substantial degree of an inadequate standard”.

He said the tribunal gave its reasons for making the recommendations before the High Court, including that the findings of misconduct were serious and went to the protection of the public. While the tribunal gave credit to Moylan for his admissions as to fact, it was of the opinion that his insight was limited.

It also noted Moylan had been practising for a long period, had no finding of misconduct until 2022 and was close to retirement.

Moylan’s previous disciplinary history, Watson said, was considered by the tribunal as an aggravating factor. The tribunal did not recommend suspension because Moylan was close to retirement and intended to wind down his practice.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[‘Everything indicates’ Web Summit will be called off tomorrow, says Lisbon mayor]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/everything-indicates-web-summit-will-be-called-off-tomorrow-says-lisbon-mayor/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/everything-indicates-web-summit-will-be-called-off-tomorrow-says-lisbon-mayor/Tue, 10 Nov 2026 17:22:13 +0000Web Summit, the Irish-founded global technology conference that has brought up to 70,000 people to Lisbon this week, may be called off on Wednesday as Portugal braces for extreme wind and rain.

Lisbon mayor Carlos Moedas, the centre-right politician who addressed the technology conference’s opening ceremony Monday night, told Portuguese reporters Tuesday afternoon “everything indicates that Web Summit will not be able to function tomorrow”.

This is ultimately a decision for the national government’s ministry for internal affairs, he said, with whom he has been in contact. “It is obvious that it is very difficult to guarantee the functioning of Web Summit tomorrow, but this situation will be brought to the level of the Ministry for Internal Affairs,” he said.

The Ministry is yet to publicly confirm a decision.

“We have people from other countries who are here. There are more than 60,000 people in a place – in the Park of Nations – where we have a river that is right next to it, where very adverse conditions will be,” Moedas said.

“I think that will be the solution [to cancel the event], but obviously it is not a decision for the Mayor of Lisbon, but everything indicates that this would be the solution,” he said.

The Portuguese Institute for the Sea and Atmosphere, the country’s weather authority akin to Met Éireann, has placed the southern half of the country under a red warning for wind, its highest alert, and the entirety of the country under yellow warning for rain.

While storms Bruna and Charles have brought rain to Portugal for most of the week, Wednesday is forecast to be the peak of the disruptionpeak, with tunnel networks, public parks and cultural venues across Lisbon ordered to close from midnight Tuesday, the mayor said.

Web Summit wrote in a statement: “We are aware of the weather warnings for Wednesday afternoon and evening and are assessing the situation with the National Emergency and Civil Protection authority and the Public Security Police.”

“We will provide further updates as soon as confirmed information becomes available,” a spokesperson said.

The Portuguese Minister of Internal Administration, Luís Neves, has also announced the closure of non-essential public services and schools across the country on Wednesday. While “closing the Lisbon Metro is not currently being considered”, he said, “everything is evolving”.

“Everyone who can, stay at home. I appeal to all employers to be understanding. Tomorrow will be an exceptional day, and it is necessary for us to remain indoors and protected,” Neves told reporters at a press conference Tuesday.

The technology conference, which was founded by businessman Paddy Cosgrave, has already attracted controversy in Lisbon, with its opening ceremony having coincided with the end of a housing rights encampment protest on one of the capital’s most prominent plazas.

Moedas had ordered the 200 or so protesters to move from Rossio Square to make room for a Christmas market. The dispute made its way through the judicial system, however, demonstrators called off the action Monday night, saying they must “enlarge the movement” and “go elsewhere”.

They have planned a counter-protest outside Web Summit for Wednesday afternoon.

]]>Patricia De Melo Moreira<![CDATA[DCC takes £348.3m charge against tech unit before sale deal]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/dcc-takes-3483m-charge-against-tech-unit-before-sale-deal/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/dcc-takes-3483m-charge-against-tech-unit-before-sale-deal/Tue, 10 Nov 2026 15:53:57 +0000DCC Energy booked a £348.3 million (€416.9 million) charge against its technology unit in the six months to the end of September as it neared a deal to sell the business.

The impairment charge pushed DCC into a net loss of £323.7 million for the period, according to its latest financial results, published on Tuesday.

The Dublin-based group, which is in the process of being taken over by US private equity firms KKR and Energy Capital Partners, said in early October that it will receive $701 million (€626.8 million) in net proceeds for the tech unit, called Nexora, which it has agreed to sell to New York-based One Equity Partners.

KKR and Energy Capital had promised as part of their deal to give DCC shareholders a £1.25-a-share payout if Nexora achieved $800 million. That was in addition to £65.25-a-share on offer for the wider group. The company’s shareholders will have to make do with a third of the £1.25 maximum additional consideration.

The deal was also well below that some analysts had initially expected the division to achieve when DCC chief executive Donal Murphy announced in late 2024 that the group was abandoning what remained of its conglomerate roots to focus on energy.

“Following the agreement to dispose of [Nexora] in October 2026, a non-cash impairment before tax of £348.3 million has been recognised in the current period to reflect the expected proceeds on disposal,” DCC said on Tuesday.

“The net charge also includes restructuring, redundancy and transaction-related costs associated with the disposal and separation of the business, and a gain of £12.7 million on the disposal of property in North America. There was a related tax credit of £24.4 million in relation to these charges.”

DCC confirmed that it expects the Nexora sale to be completed by March 1st and the KKR and Energy Capital takeover to be finalised “in the first quarter” of 2027.

]]>Nick Bradshaw for The Irish Times<![CDATA[Northern envy at Republic pay rates]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/politics/2026/11/10/northern-envy-at-republic-pay-rates/https://www.irishtimes.com/politics/2026/11/10/northern-envy-at-republic-pay-rates/Tue, 10 Nov 2026 14:05:42 +0000Angela McGowan, the director general of the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) in Northern Ireland, watched TV news reports on Monday night on the pay offer to public servants in the Republic.

“I just couldn’t believe it. I was thinking of my poor members on the Border, if they have to keep up with this. And I don’t even know if it was accepted,” she said about the then 10.5 per cent pay offer on the table.

McGowan’s incredulity was displayed at the launch in the Royal Irish Academy in Dublin of a major report by the CBI, the Dublin-based employers’ group, Ibec and recruitment firm Hays.

The North/South pay gap is one of many issues affecting the all-island jobs market, particularly for Northern organisations on the Border unable to compete with better-paid and easy-to-get-to jobs just a few kilometres away.

For Eileen O’Malley of The Wheel, which has with European Union help recently created the first all-island alliance of charities, community groups and social enterprises, the issue is a daily problem.

In the alliance’s first few meetings, recruitment, taxes and pay issues across the island have been flagged again and again, with people living just a few kilometres apart getting dramatically different wages.

Four-year-old figures suggest 18,000 people cross the Border daily for work, though, in reality, the number has grown dramatically in the years since – especially in construction.

However, there are complications aplenty for employers, especially in hiring workers who want to work remotely – since cross-Border tax laws have not fully caught up with hybrid working.

“There is a groundswell of frustration, particularly since Covid, but even before that,” Fergal O’Brien of Ibec declared, “particularly in the Border areas who have been really active on this agenda.”

“Some companies are saying that unfortunately they can now no longer hire cross-Border because they are worried about tax compliance issues,” said O’Brien, adding the issues went beyond tax.

McGowan agreed, pointing out that differences in Irish and UK pensions rules cause real complications: “Unless your pension is recognised in the UK, you’re not entitled to relief there.”

The headaches for HR departments are illustrated by someone who works four days in Dublin and one day at home in Northern Ireland paying southern income tax for the days spent in Dublin.

Such a person is liable for UK tax on all income, with credit for Irish taxes paid. Equally, they are liable for Irish PRSI, but not UK national insurance if they work for a day at home – but they are if they work two days at home.

Top-up tax bills are a particular issue for people from the North working in the Republic, with more than half surveyed for the report saying such bills were a deterrent.

Less than a third of people in the Republic working in Northern Ireland find top-ups such a fear because southern tax rules offer cross-Border workers’ relief, removing foreign earnings from Irish income tax liability.

For McGowan, things do not have to be exactly the same: “But they do need to be aligned so that two payrolls, two regulatory systems can work as close as possible together.”

The difficulties facing employers increase with foreign-born staff, since they do not enjoy the same Common Travel Area rights as do Irish and British citizens, even if they are legally living in the Republic.

One in five people working in the Republic is not an Irish citizen, but such employees could not be stationed by their employers in Northern Ireland-based operations.

“That’s a real practical day-to-day challenge for some firms, who need to have a single organisational chart. They don’t have that ability within their own teams,” said O’Brien.

Making cross-Border hiring easier brings all sorts of advantages, said O’Brien: “This is a really in-depth piece of research. The bit that jumps off the page for me is how tight our labour markets are.

“Things are exceptionally tight. Hiring managers say that over two-thirds of them believe the skills that they need are available on the other side of the Border. That’s really, really significant.

“That demonstrates the untapped potential there. The skills are out there. We need to work harder to make sure that they’re fully accessible, and that the all-island labour market functions well,” he said.

Knowledge is everything, the research shows. Half of those in firms that have hired cross-Border think of the island as a whole when they think about recruitment.

Yet just a fifth of those in firms that have never done so think the same.

]]><![CDATA[Cost of residential land in Dublin nearly triple national median]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/cost-of-residential-land-in-dublin-nearly-triple-national-median/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/cost-of-residential-land-in-dublin-nearly-triple-national-median/Tue, 10 Nov 2026 13:02:59 +0000Residentially zoned land in Dublin commanded nearly three times the price paid for land in other parts of the country last year, according to the Central Statistics Office (CSO).

The median, or middle value, price paid for an acre of residential development land in Dublin in 2025 was €721,288.

This compared with a national median price of €258,716.

Land in Dublin and its commuter counties typically commands a premium because of the population concentration.

Dublin and the southwest region – Cork and Kerry – had the highest median prices per acre in 2025, at €721,288 and €469,061, respectively.

The Border region had the lowest regional median, at €122,300 per acre.

By county, Kerry had the highest published median price per acre in 2025, at €727,053, followed by Dublin at €721,288 and Galway at €470,723.

However, the Kerry figure appears to have been inflated by a small number of high-value transactions.

Leitrim had the lowest published county median, at €71,894 per acre

The value of residential land sold last year amounted to €217.9 million, the CSO said.

The greatest recorded volume of land sold was in the mideast – Kildare, Louth, Meath and Wicklow – at 103.3 acres. The midlands recorded the lowest volume, at 24.6 acres.

The CSO noted that the value and volume of transactions included in its release did not represent all residentially zoned land sales. “Only transactions where the land area could be verified at the time of sale are included,” it said.

Individuals accounted for more than two-thirds – 72.3 per cent – of vendors by number of transactions in 2025, while construction companies accounted for 68.5 per cent of the value of land purchased.

Construction companies bought just a third of the land sold for housing last year

In 2025, land subject to the residentially zoned land tax had a median price per acre of €329,896, compared with €184,421 for land not subject to the tax, a difference of about 79 per cent.

“This is a descriptive comparison and does not establish that the tax caused the price difference,” the agency said.

The latest snapshot of house prices from the CSO will be published next week. It is expected to show that the market here is cooling with purchasing power impacted by higher borrowing costs.

The latest numbers for the month of August put inflation (for prices paid) at 5.1 per cent and at 3.9 per cent in Dublin.

The CSO’s numbers are based on stamp duty data from Revenue and reflect transactions that took place at least two months ago; as a result there is a lag.

The Irish property market is undergoing something of a reset in the face of higher borrowing costs, persistent supply shortages and changes to the rental rules.

]]>Francesco Scatena<![CDATA[At Web Summit opener, Palestine gets a brief mention and the loudest cheer]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/at-web-summits-opener-palestine-gets-a-brief-mention-and-the-loudest-cheer/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/at-web-summits-opener-palestine-gets-a-brief-mention-and-the-loudest-cheer/Mon, 09 Nov 2026 20:14:16 +0000Paddy Cosgrave welcomed thousands of Web Summit early arrivals to Lisbon on Monday night, telling them the future of technology was “increasingly Chinese”, with “more than 50 superstars from China’s leading AI labs” attending the technology conference.

“This year’s Web Summit has, without a doubt in my mind, the most important line-up of technology speakers we have ever had,” he said. “They are not from California – they are from China, because Chinese companies are building more for our shared futures than companies from anywhere else. This is just a fact.

“We’re of course grateful to have speakers and partners like Apple, Meta and Google – they are the prominent technology companies of today,” Cosgrave said as he stood alone on stage, with two jumbo-screens of his face bookending the Web Summit logo. “These companies are all, almost without exception, started in California.

“But, increasingly, the superstars of the future are not coming from California, they’re coming from China. They’re the future stars in AI, in robotics, in cars . . . in energy and in so much more.”

Kicking off the opening ceremony was a two-minute dance routine performed by nine humanoid robots created by the Chinese company AgiBot.

Agibot robots swept athletics categories in the first world Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing three months ago.

More than 100 Irish start-ups head to Web Summit alongside largest-ever Chinese delegation

Addressing the crowd gathered in the centre stage of the MEO Arena, Cosgrave wore a speckled moss green Aran jumper. It looked strikingly similar to a jumper that is available to buy for €895 from his wife Faye Dinsmore’s fashion brand.

This one, however, was more bespoke than an off-the-rack knit. It had the phrase “keep the triple lock” stitched across its chest in a not-so-subtle reminder of Cosgrave’s view on the Government’s recent move to reform the traditional pillars of the State’s military neutrality.

Appealing to his techie audience, the triple lock was represented with three padlock emojis.

The mere mention of Palestine would deliver a less predictable gauge of audience views. Three years ago, Cosgrave resigned as chief executive of Web Summit amid controversy caused by him tweeting: “War crimes are war crimes even when committed by allies, and should be called out for what they are.”

Two weeks after Hamas’s attacks of October 7th, 2023, Cosgrave’s condemnation of Israel’s assault on Gaza prompted international companies to withdraw from the high-profile tech conference.

He returned to his post six months later. On Monday, 2½ years on from Cosgrave’s return as chief executive, Casey Lau – host for the first night – decided to roll the dice. Lau shouted out “Palestine” in acknowledgment of one of the countries that has sent start-up delegations to the conference.

“We have people from Paraguay, from Pakistan, from Palestine . . .” he said, trailing off in suspense (or nervousness). But the gamble paid off. It garnered the loudest cheer of the night.

Lau tried to follow up with its flag-bearer – who walked alongside a man carrying the Irish Tricolour in a parade of nationalities represented at the conference – to ask him what his start-up’s purpose is, but to no avail.

]]>Patricia De Melo Moreira<![CDATA[Situation ‘grim’ after State-backed medtech start-up suffered delays bringing products to market]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/situation-grim-after-state-backed-medtech-start-up-suffered-delays-bringing-products-to-market/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/situation-grim-after-state-backed-medtech-start-up-suffered-delays-bringing-products-to-market/Tue, 10 Nov 2026 12:38:35 +0000The situation at an Enterprise Ireland-backed medtech firm last year was “very grim” after delays in bringing its products to market, with shareholders warning that funding might not be forthcoming, its chief executive has said.

The senior executive was giving evidence at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) on Monday on complaints alleging unlawful non-payment of wages and constructive dismissal by a senior software developer.

Hammad Ul Ahad is pursuing complaints under the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977 and the Payment of Wages Act 1991 against his former employer, Amnexis Holding Ltd, a Dublin-based software developer.

The firm is involved in developing virtual assistance and transcription software for use by medical professionals, the WRC was told.

Ul Ahad’s case is that from the start of July 2025, his hours and pay were cut by 50 per cent in what he said had been a “unilateral” decision by the company. He quit after four months on half pay, the tribunal heard.

“I couldn’t work under the enforced conditions. I was facing severe financial difficulties; the contract was already void,” Ul Ahad said.

The sum in dispute in the pay claim was not specified during the hearing. Ul Ahad’s evidence was that he was supporting two families in his home country of Pakistan.

He accepted under cross-examination by John Madden, instructed by Kate O’Brien of Hogan Dowling McNamara Solicitors for the respondent, that there was a clause in his job contract providing for lay-off and short-time working.

His position was that this was meant to be in the event of a short-term shortage of work. Ul Ahad said, however, that the decision to cut his hours was a “financial shareholder strategy” with “no clear timeline” and was “clearly not a temporary shortage of work”.

The company’s founder and chief executive, Joachim Mueller-Wende, said in his evidence that the firm in early 2025 was in “a very grim situation”.

The company’s position was that the development of new app features was stalled for most of that year because of difficulties with its underlying data architecture, though Ul Ahad disputed this.

There had been “some good results” from tests of its virtual assistant app, Eva, at Germany’s largest hospital that had started in October 2023, Mueller-Wende said.

However, Eva was not ready to go to market, and the company had decided bring out a stand-alone transcription app for use by medical professionals, which it called Quixxs, Mueller-Wende told the WRC.

“So, being late launching Quixxs – some competitors had been there a year earlier – and not having been able to create Eva to go to market either, we were facing a very grim situation at the start of 2025,” Mueller-Wende said.

In particular, Mueller-Wende said there was “overcapacity” in back-end development work on Quixxs, which was Ul Ahad’s area, and he could see “no other candidate to cut back”.

He said Ul Ahad “agreed with me to accept the period of cutting down” with the proviso that it start in July 2025, and not in June that year as originally proposed. Ul Ahad strongly disputed this.

Adjudication officer Orla Jones closed the hearing and is expected to give her decision in writing on Ul Ahad’s complaints in due course.

]]>Issarawat Tattong<![CDATA[‘Easy scapegoat’ for news publishers to blame AI for low readership, media executive says]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/easy-scapegoat-for-news-publishers-to-blame-ai-for-low-readership-media-executive-says/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/10/easy-scapegoat-for-news-publishers-to-blame-ai-for-low-readership-media-executive-says/Tue, 10 Nov 2026 14:11:03 +0000Services powered by artificial intelligence (AI) have become “an easy scapegoat” for news publishers to blame for their decreasing reader numbers, a leading media executive has said at Web Summit, with changes in more traditional online algorithms acting as the “main function” behind the decline.

“We don’t see any loss of subscriptions because of AI – we are still increasing our portfolio of subscribers,” said Louis Dreyfus, the group chief executive of Le Monde, which publishes in both English and French.

“We don’t explain a decrease in audience with AI, the change in algorithm discovery is the main function in the decrease – but not AI,” Dreyfus, who has worked for the French newspaper since 2010, added.

The new technology “offers an easy scapegoat for the publisher to say ‘it’s not us, it’s AI’” when addressing the industry’s challenges, he said.

Le Monde holds a multiyear licensing agreement and training programme with OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, to allow the chatbot to access the newspaper’s archives and current reporting when responding to questions and prompts.

“This agreement is historic as it is the first signed between a French media organisation and a major player in this nascent industry,” the publisher wrote in a 2024 statement announcing the deal. It “is further recognition of the reliability of the work of our editorial team”, it added.

More than 100 Irish start-ups head to Web Summit alongside largest-ever Chinese delegation

Speaking to hundreds of Web Summit attendees on Tuesday, Dreyfus continued: “What we’ve seen with our partnership with, let’s say for example, OpenAI [is] we use this new audience that is coming from ChatGPT to Le Monde, because there was an answer made with Le Monde or Le Monde was quoted in it. They’re coming to us and it’s converting into subscriptions.”

How will it affect the Government’s fiscal position?

The rule of thumb is that each 1 per cent hike in the public sector pay and pensions bill costs the exchequer roughly €370 million.

So the Government’s fiscal position would be €800 million worse than forecast in 2027. The additional pay bumps for 2028 and 2029 are also not factored in. That additional money will have to come out of tax resources and will reduce the Government’s budget surpluses over the period.

On the other side of the ledger, the State’s financial position is expected to be boosted by corporate tax receipts, which are predicted to rise to €45 billion by 2030.

Private sector wages have outpaced those in the public sector since 2008. According to the official data, private sector wages are up by between 52-56 per cent over that period versus 25 per cent in the public sector.

They also insist there are acute labour shortages in education and healthcare and argue that a lacklustre deal will worsen the exodus of young nurses and teachers.

This later deadline undoubtedly applies to most people – according to Revenue, 98 per cent of Form 11s were filed electronically last year, for the 2024 tax year.

But if you’re a landlord, director, have €5,000 or more in taxable non-PAYE income, or are self-employed and have yet to file, what do you need to know about this year’s returns? And most importantly perhaps, will you pay less tax this time around?

Will my tax bill fall?

A number of tax changes were made for 2025, which means that if you’re paying tax for this year now, your total bill should decline, all other things being equal.

The biggest gain is probably among those earning more than €42,000 (for a single person), thanks to a €2,000 increase in the standard rate band. This means a reduction in tax of about €400 a year.

And there was also an increase, of €125, in the earned income tax credit for the self-employed, which increased to €2,000, as well as changes to the universal social charge (USC), where the 4 per cent rate will fall back to 3 per cent, and will apply on earnings of €27,382 to €70,044.

For example, based on figures from PwC, a dual income family earning €175,000 would have had a net monthly income of €9,146 in 2024, but €9,245 in 2025, so savings of €99 a month or €1,188 a year.

One tax that did go up, however, was PRSI; last year it increased by 0.1 per cent. And looking ahead, PRSI increased again this October, by 0.15 per cent.

If you’re renting or own a home

“Check the mortgage interest tax credit and the rent tax credit, as both are often missed,” says Kinga Guzikowska, of KPG Accounting Services.

It may be due to come to an end this year – no extension was granted in last month’s budget – but those filing for 2025 might still qualify for the mortgage interest tax credit.

To do so, you will need to have had an outstanding mortgage balance of between €80,000 and €500,000 as of end-2022 and, crucially, you must have paid more in interest on your loan in 2025 than you did in 2022.

It’s unlikely to change the dial on your return, however; the relief is capped at 20 per cent of the increase, up to a maximum of €1,250. As an example, a €3,000 increase would give a tax saving of €300.

For renters, the rent tax credit increased to €1,000 for a single person (€2,000 for a couple) for 2025, and can make a meaningful impact on your tax bill, so if you’re liable for it, make sure you file for it. Remember, if you’re paying for your child’s digs or student room, the credit also applies. Latest figures for 2024 show that more than 335,000 taxpayers claimed the relief that year.

If you rented out a property in 2025, you will pay slightly less tax this year than you might have done previously, due to the increase in the Residential Premises Rental Income Relief.

First introduced in 2024, the relief is offered at a rate of 20 per cent of the landlord’s rental income. For 2025 tax returns, the limit will increase from €3,000 to €4,000. Not only that, but as the limit will increase to €5,000 for the 2026 tax year, you can also get a reduction on your preliminary tax for that year.

It means that the maximum credit will increase from €600 for 2024 to €800 in 2025 – and €1,000 for 2026 and 2027.

Even at the high-water mark of construction in 2006, when a record 92,000 homes were built, property prices surged by 14 per cent. Back then the cost of construction was also soaring despite the fact we had an extra 100,000 construction workers in the country.

Eurostat’s latest house price-to-income ratio report, published on Monday, suggests this detachment is continuing.

The growth in house prices relative to income in Ireland between 2015 and 2025 was estimated at 14.4 per cent, more than double the EU average (6.8 per cent), the report reveals.

At the other end, Romania recorded the largest decrease (-42.8 per cent), followed by Finland (-25.2 per cent) and Bulgaria (-16.2 per cent).

Top finance officials worried about billions in debt racked up by housing bodies

“These figures compare price changes relative to income changes over time; as such, they do not rank countries by how expensive homes are in relation to income levels in absolute terms,” Eurostat said.

Rent supports and help-to-buy schemes are being used as stop-gaps as more and more would-be buyers get priced out of the market. ]]>David Davies<![CDATA[Marrying after retirement will deprive spouse of survivor’s pension]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/10/marrying-after-retirement-will-deprive-spouse-of-survivors-pension/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/10/marrying-after-retirement-will-deprive-spouse-of-survivors-pension/Tue, 10 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000My query relates to an occupational pension of my husband and my lack of entitlement to half of this if he were to pre-decease me.

JN

Public service pensions in general make provision for a 50 per cent survivor’s pension for a spouse if the retired public servant predeceases them. It is a valuable safety net for families .

But you appear to have lost out which I certainly agree sounds very unfair.

Following an enquiry from you, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage sent you what appear to be disembodied section from various bits of legislation that are as impenetrable as this stuff usually is.

The issue here is that there are two schemes - an original one that dates back to 1956 legislation and a more recent one operating under legislation passed in the 1980s. What rights you do and do not have depend on which one covers your husband’s employment.

I am indebted to Irish Congress of Trade Unions head of social policy and employment affairs, Laura Bambrick, and a number of her colleagues in Ictu’s public service unions for guiding me through the relevant detail.

Essentially, under the original 1956 Local Government (Superannuation) Act, there was no provision for a survivor’s pension under the widow’s and orphan pension scheme in a case like yours - where you got married after your husband had retired from his public sector role.

That scheme was specifically designed to cover family relationships established during pensionable employment. Once the person was no longer contributing to the scheme - as they would not in retirement - they were not covered for any marriage that took place during their working lives, nor any child born.

However, that changed in the 1980s.

People working in the Civil Service who were appointed after September 1st, 1984 became members of a revised spouses’ and children’s pension scheme. And this scheme made specific provision that even where a marriage took place after retirement, the spouse would be entitled to a survivors’ pension.

Those pension rights were extended to local authority staff under the Local Government Officers (Spouses and Children’s Contributory Pension) Scheme, 1986, with the rights backdated to September 1st, 1984.

This is interesting because it shows that as far back as 1984, there was an understanding that there was a reasonable case for extending pension protection to spouses who, simply by accident of timing, got married after a person’s retirement.

So, if your husband started working with the local authority any time after the end of August 1984, you are entitled to a pension on the back of his employment in the event of his death.

Even if he started working with them before that date, there was an option at that time for existing employees to transfer to the new scheme. He and you would certainly need to check through his records to see if he availed of that opportunity or chose to stay with the original scheme.

The response you have got from the department does not seem to clarify that one way or the other. And one of the trade union sources notes that Article 120 of the 1998 Local Government Superannuation (Consolidation) Scheme, which was quoted to you by the Department of Housing, relates to the older Widows’ and Orphans’ arrangements.

If he was covered under the newer arrangements, it would be irrelevant.

So, first up, track down the dates when your husband started work with the local authority and when he retired. If he was employed with them before 1984, you also need to check whether he opted in to the revised arrangements that came into force at that time, or not.

I am told that the pensions section in the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation may be able to help.

And what about the fairness issue? It does seem harsh that, having accepted the argument as far back as 1984 that marriages after retirement should be recognised, you could find yourself left with no survivor’s pension more than 40 years later.

That doesn’t necessarily mean that it breaches current legislation of equality but it does suggest that a rethink in Government might be timely. There cannot be that many people in your position so the financial impact on the exchequer is hardly an issue.

]]>RuslanDashinsky<![CDATA[AI agents in car dealerships: No time off and they work out how quickly a vehicle will sell]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/ai-agents-in-car-dealerships-they-never-take-time-off-or-get-sick-and-can-work-out-how-quickly-vehicles-will-sell/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/ai-agents-in-car-dealerships-they-never-take-time-off-or-get-sick-and-can-work-out-how-quickly-vehicles-will-sell/Mon, 09 Nov 2026 05:47:00 +0000Car sales, to the buyer at least, haven’t changed all that much since Henry Ford first rolled out the Model T. It’s a human business. One that involves talking to customers, assessing vehicles, deciding what stock to buy and avoid, and, of course, closing sales. On the face of it, this is hardly the poster child for disruption by artificial intelligence (AI).

Yet AI is making an impact, with several Irish companies at the forefront of that movement, with Irish dealers embracing the time benefits that come with deploying AI agents.

For the dealership, the goal is to capture and keep the buyer’s attention while their interest is at its peak.

“The customer wants the car. There are probably a few versions of the car available. The first person that responds and captures their time will most likely bring them in and sell them the car,” he says.

The long road to building an Irish AI start-up

AutoAgent deployed Aran, its bespoke agent, with Tony Burke Motors to engage with customers when humans weren’t on hand.

“It’s a response optimisation platform that responds to customers and captures their interest while it’s at its peak. It never takes time off, is never sick, and responds the way your dealership wants with your process,” he says.

Would you trust this AI to sell you a second-hand car?

“Speed isn’t the major concern because a normal consumer is willing to wait a few seconds. They are focused mostly on accurate and relevant information that they can verify. A fast answer doesn’t always mean it’s a good answer,” says Janet Xiu Shi, an AI quality evaluation adviser.

Peter Thiel-backed AI company Cognition establishes Irish presence

The value goes beyond the individual sale to the broader decisions that a dealership wants to make. AI’s value goes beyond customer service work – indeed, quite a lot of it isn’t customer facing at all. It can aid dealerships working out what vehicles to acquire and how quickly they will sell.

So, not surprisingly, the result was a big influx of workers from these countries.

However, since 2004 there has been very rapid growth in the economies of the states that joined the EU at that time, increasing the earnings of those who stay or return home. Pay in sectors such as IT, financial services, pharmaceuticals and medicine are much higher in the Republic than in eastern Europe. However, these jobs require proficiency in English, favouring countries where English language proficiency is more widespread.

So, in more recent years, skills shortages in the State have increasingly been met from outside the EU. Our ageing population is leading to greater demands on our hospitals and social care system. While EU workers can work here freely, most migrants from outside the EU require work permits. “By simply reviewing your existing arrangements, you can identify possible gaps and make more informed decisions. The earlier people take this step, the more time they will have to plan for the retirement they want.”

The findings broadly reflect a survey by Aviva in recent days which found that almost two in three people over the age of 50 fear their retirement savings – State pension, workplace or private pension and investment income – will not last throughout their retirement.

A similar number of retirees told the Aviva study that, given the chance, they would have changed something about how they prepared.

While people are not sure what their pension fund will pay them, they are fairly confident that a shortfall in those funds means they will end up working longer than they had planned.

Irish workers, on average, would like to retire at the age of 61, according to the AIB survey, but they expect to keep working until 66. Young workers have slightly higher expectations but also fear the shortfall may be greater. They would ideally retire at 58, they say, but expect to work a further six years, until they are 64.

Despite those concerns, retirement planning is struggling to compete with more immediate priorities. Respondents told Amárach, which spoke to a nationally representative sample of 2,000 adults over the age of 25 for the study, that they were more likely to have thought about planning a holiday over the past 12 months (47 per cent) than about planning for retirement (22 per cent).

Ryan said that while retirement may feel distant or difficult to navigate, understanding existing pension arrangements and the income they could provide is an important step towards assessing whether retirement plans are on track.

Across all questions in the survey, women are in a less favourable position than men.

]]>Alihan Usullu

Poland has detained and charged two Ukrainian citizens accused of carrying out espionage and acts of sabotage on behalf of Russia.

The men, aged 24 and 25, were allegedly paid to conduct reconnaissance of critical infrastructure and military facilities across Poland. They are also accused of setting fire to several vehicles with the aim of stoking anti-Ukrainian sentiment.

Funkcjonariusze Agencji Bezpieczeństwa Wewnętrznego zatrzymali w Mińsku Mazowieckim dwóch obywateli Ukrainy w wieku 24 i 25 lat podejrzanych o szpiegostwo i prowadzenie działań dywersyjnych na zlecenie rosyjskich służb specjalnych.
▶️ Mężczyźni rozpoznawali i robili zdjęcia… pic.twitter.com/G3i8hEsBHT

— Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 10, 2026

The suspects were detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) on 3 November in Mińsk Mazowiecki, a town just outside Warsaw, the capital. ABW officers also searched their residences and other locations connected to the investigation, seizing data storage devices and narcotics.

According to investigators, the suspects were tasked with setting vehicles on fire after changing their licence plates to ones used by Ukrainian military vehicles. This was “aimed at fueling anti-Ukrainian sentiment”, says the National Prosecutor’s Office.

Prosecutors have charged the men under Poland’s espionage law with working against Poland on behalf of a foreign intelligence service – a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of five years – and sabotage on behalf of foreign intelligence, which is punishable by 10 years to life.

At the prosecutor’s request, a court ordered both suspects to be placed in pretrial detention for three months.

 

In recent years, Poland has seen a huge rise in cases of espionage and sabotage carried out on behalf of Russia.

The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined.

Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe.

Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026

Last month, a Polish man was jailed for five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of an airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland.

Shortly afterwards, the trial began of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders.

In July, a Russian married couple with refugee status in Poland were convicted of working as spies on behalf of Moscow. In October, a member of Poland’s military reserve, who holds both Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, was detained on suspicion of espionage.

]]> “Strong traces of right-wing extremism” in activity of Kraków terrorist, says justice minister https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/10/strong-traces-of-right-wing-extremism-in-activity-of-krakow-terrorist-says-justice-minister/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 11:17:52 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106614

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Poland’s justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, says that investigators have so far found “very strong traces of right-wing extremism” in the activity of Michał Oksiński, the man who carried out Saturday’s mass terrorist shooting in Kraków that left six people dead.

The perpetrator’s search history included websites relating to Anders Breivik, the Norwegian far-right terrorist who killed 77 people during two attacks in 2011.

Żurek’s comments come amid intense debate and dispute in Poland over the beliefs and motives of Oksiński, who on Monday died from the injuries he sustained during a shootout with police that brought his rampage to an end.

W. Żurek ujawnia nowe ustalenia po zamachu w Krakowie. Tłumik w samochodzie sprawcy i ślady zainteresowania Breivikiemhttps://t.co/nd1XPBlmrI

— Radio Kraków (@RadioKrakow) November 10, 2026

On Tuesday, Żurek, who also serves as prosecutor general, spoke to local broadcaster Radio Kraków about the progress of the investigation into Oksiński. He confirmed that the perpetrator had not left behind any letter or other kind of message revealing his motives.

“Those motives are being investigated,” said the minister. “There are very strong traces of right-wing extremism. I can already confirm some information because the services have access to the perpetrator’s computer. Indeed, visits to websites related to Anders Breivik are visible.”

Żurek also pointed to the fact that, as prosecutors announced on Sunday, a so-called Gadsden flag (showing a snake above the words “Don’t tread on me”) had been found in Oksiński’s home.

Prosecutors say a "Don't Tread on Me" flag was found hanging at the home of the perpetrator of the attack in Kraków

They emphasise that the flag is not associated with any one ideology or organisation and that they are still trying to determine the shooter's motives and beliefs pic.twitter.com/yoNfh7cHwU

— Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) November 9, 2026

Although the National Prosecutor’s Office emphasised that the flag is not associated with any one ideology or organisation, Żurek noted that it was displayed during the attack on the United States Capitol by supporters of Donald Trump in 2021.

“We know well that during the attack on the Capitol, there were quite a few of these flags among far-right groups in the United States,” said the minister. “This flag [in Oksiński’s home] also sends a signal to the security services and the prosecutor’s office.”

Żurek added that a search of the perpetrator’s workplace had also identified “symbolism there that could point to this thread [of right-wing extremism]”, but provided no further details.

The minister noted, however, that investigators are also taking into account the potential for “mental disorders” playing a role in the actions of Oksiński, whose parents and sister were found shot dead in his home.

 

Żurek’s remarks come following controversy in Poland over a statement by interior minister Marcin Kierwiński on Saturday, in the immediate aftermath of the attack, when he said that early indications suggest that Oksiński had held “very radical views”, including a “fascination with far-right ideologies”.

Over the following two days, Kierwiński refused to provide evidence supporting those claims, and in a TV interview on Sunday evening said that he had simply been sharing “first hypotheses”.

That led some right-wing opposition politicians and commentators to accuse Kierwiński of spreading false claims, either through incompetence or as a deliberate attempt to associate the attack with the right.

However, speaking to Radio Kraków on Tuesday, Żurek said that “it seems that what Minister Kierwiński communicated in those first hours is confirmed by the evidence”.

Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, is facing growing pressure to present evidence to back his claim that the Kraków shooter was driven by far-right ideologies, amid criticism from opposition parties that he is seeking to exploit the tragedy for political reasons.

— Jakub Krupa (@JakubKrupa) November 9, 2026

On social media, many people have also been sharing alleged images of Oksiński’s past activities, both online and in real life, claiming that they show he held left-wing views.

However, some of those images have proven to be false, such as one purporting to show him at a pro-refugee rally (the photograph is genuine, but the person in it was not Oksiński) and another purporting to show him shaking hands with Kierwiński (the image was AI-generated).

Further alleged images from Oskiński’s social media accounts remain unverified and also depict posts that were made six or seven years ago.

Another fake that is being widely shared.

While the photo is genuine, the person highlighted is not the Kraków shooter.

Other images from the event clearly show it isn't him, while fact-checkers @konkret24 actually tracked down the guy in the photo: https://t.co/4HeofUdOUm pic.twitter.com/pTfdkCZlAL

— Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) November 9, 2026

On Monday, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski told Polsat News that there had been an “enormous wave of disinformation” in the wake of Saturday’s tragedy. He criticised “pseudo-journalists and politicians” who had shared such content.

“Digital platforms acted very responsibly, removing this content quickly,” said Gawkowski. However, he added that X, the social media service owned by Elon Musk, had been an exception and was “where the most radicalisation occurred”.

Meanwhile, the interior ministry’s spokeswoman, Karolina Gałecka, announced on Monday that they would notify prosecutors about the creation and dissemination of the AI-generated image of Kierwiński shaking hands with Oksiński.

She said it had been spread by social media accounts associated with right-wing broadcaster Republika.

]]> What is at stake in Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal dispute? https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/10/what-is-at-stake-in-polands-constitutional-tribunal-dispute/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 09:32:10 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106606 Aleks Szczerbiak The escalating conflict has become a struggle over who defines constitutional legitimacy.]]>

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Poland’s escalating Constitutional Tribunal (TK) dispute is no longer simply a legal argument about contested appointments but a struggle over who defines constitutional legitimacy.

As the liberal-centrist government and right-wing opposition and president advance rival rule-of-law claims, the conflict risks entrenching a system of legal dualism in which judicial authority depends on political allegiance rather than broad constitutional consent.

The roots of the crisis

Poland’s 15-member TK is a powerful body that rules on the constitutionality of the country’s laws. The roots of the current dispute trace back to late 2015 and began immediately prior to the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party taking office following its October parliamentary election victory.

In its final weeks in power, the outgoing government, led by the liberal-centrist Civic Platform (PO, now Civic Coalition: KO), fast-tracked the appointment of five tribunal members who were replacing those whose terms were set to expire in November and December.

Upon winning an outright parliamentary majority, the incoming PiS-led government refused to recognise these appointments, elected a slate of five new tribunal members, and party-backed President Andrzej Duda swore them in.

Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025

The tribunal (still largely composed of pre-2015 judges) ruled that three of the outgoing parliament’s appointments were lawful, so only two of the new ones could stand. PiS refused to accept this, creating the so-called “understudy” judges (dublerzy) controversy.

As further vacancies arose, the new parliament gradually installed its nominees, culminating in the appointment at the end of 2016 of one of them, Julia Przyłębska, as tribunal president. Przyłębska’s leadership was contested on procedural grounds, as was that of her 2024 successor Bogdan Święczkowski, a former senior prosecutor closely aligned with the 2015-23 PiS administration.

All of this led to the then-opposition parties and much of the Polish legal and the EU political establishments denouncing the tribunal as legally compromised and politically captured.

Total non-cooperation

Following the autumn 2023 parliamentary election, a new coalition government headed up by KO leader Donald Tusk embraced a policy of total non-cooperation with the tribunal, refusing to publish its rulings.

The battle for control took a new turn when, after initially not filling any tribunal vacancies, from March 2026 onwards the new parliament elected successive waves of new members, reaching eight by September.

However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki (who succeeded Duda in August 2025) refused to swear in five of these nominees, including former minister and close Tusk ally Maciej Berek. In response, the government took the unprecedented step of swearing in the contested nominees directly in parliament, a move that both Nawrocki and Święczkowski rejected as illegal.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

The conflict escalated sharply at the end of last month, when, backed by the government and tribunal members elected by the current parliamentary majority, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the five contested nominees but having the longest judicial tenure, asserted her seniority to order a one-month suspension of Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański in their official duties and assumed temporary control.

Justice minister Waldemar Żurek submitted requests to lift Święczkowski and Sochański’s immunity as the newly appointed members, and the new nominees entered the tribunal building under State Protection Service (UOP) escort.

This triggered protests by right-wing opposition supporters at the building’s gates, prompting a heavy police presence and tense stand-off. The severity of this was underscored when Nawrocki cut short an official visit to Senegal mid-flight, returned to Warsaw and entered the tribunal building in the early hours, condemning what he described as a violation of the constitutional order.

During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court.

The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026

Korwin-Piotrowska then convened a tribunal general assembly which critics argued lacked the legally required two-thirds quorum because only eight of its 15 nominal members (the newly elected ones, including the five who had not taken the presidential oath) attended.

Her supporters maintained that the quorum was met because the suspension of Święczkowski and Sochański, and exclusion of the last remaining “understudy” judge, reduced the pool of eligible members to 12.

The government’s “transitional justice” logic

For the Tusk government and its legal defenders, these exceptional executive and parliamentary countermeasures were framed through the logic of “transitional justice”: as painful and extraordinary but necessary to restore the rule of law after PiS had violated the constitution and European standards, systematically packing the tribunal with political loyalists.

Justifying its non-recognition of tribunal rulings, the government argued that the presence of three defectively elected “understudy” members and their successors, together with Przyłębska’s and Święczkowski’s procedurally flawed presidential appointments, fundamentally “contaminated” the entire body, thereby invalidating its rulings.

In its efforts to restore democracy, the government may sometimes take actions that are “not fully compliant with the law”, admits @donaldtusk.

But he says this is because of the legal chaos deliberately created by the former PiS government https://t.co/AWlM6hRLie

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 11, 2024

To provide what it argued was authoritative external confirmation of this defect, the government relied heavily on landmark European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) and EU Court of Justice (CJEU) rulings which determined that, thus constituted, the tribunal could no longer be considered a legitimate body established by legal standards.

From this perspective, refusing to recognise the tribunal’s allegedly unlawful rulings was framed as the only available mechanism to neutralise a partisan weapon that PiS had left behind to block the government’s legislative agenda.

Alternative parliamentary swearing-in procedures were justified on the grounds that the president’s role in receiving oaths was purely ceremonial, not a constitutionally mandated requirement.

 

Despite his recent political role, Berek’s appointment was defended on the basis that he played more of a technocratic-expert role within the government, and was highly qualified to undertake the extraordinary transitional measures required to repair a damaged institution.

Defenders of the tribunal leadership’s suspension and occupation of its headquarters argued that by blocking the new nominees from taking up their roles, Święczkowski had paralysed the institution and decisive measures were necessary to restore its proper functioning.

A “coup d’état”?

PiS and Nawrocki, on the other hand, maintained that the Tusk government’s actions amounted to an authoritarian attempt to operate completely outside of constitutional powers, treating legality as an option when it conflicted with its political agenda.

They insisted that all of its 2015 appointments were in full accordance with the law, correcting an improper attempt by the outgoing PO-dominated parliament to entrench its influence after electoral defeat, and that the tribunal’s ruling on the legality of these three “understudy” judges went beyond its jurisdiction.

Successive tribunal general assemblies, they argued, validly and legally selected Przyłębska and then Święczkowski as presidents, and the Tusk government had no constitutional right to pick and choose which tribunal rulings it would recognise. They said that, by delaying the election of some new members when vacancies arose, the government violated existing procedures.

The constitution, they said, explicitly required these new nominees to take their oaths directly “before the president” and that by conducting improper parliamentary swearing-in ceremonies they had effectively renounced their offices.

The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”

But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026

The candidacy of Berek, a recently active politician with doubtful professional qualifications, they said represented its own form of institutional capture and selective legality.

The suspension of the tribunal leadership and occupation of its headquarters amounted to an unlawful power grab or “coup d’état” that completely disregarded established constitutional procedures.

PiS rejected the “contamination” thesis and argued vigorously that Poland had never transferred jurisdiction over the organisation of the national judiciary to EU institutions and European courts, who had no authority to evaluate the legality of tribunal appointments.

They accused the EU political establishment of double standards, weaponising “rule-of-law” arguments to help a politically aligned government while ignoring the Tusk administration’s own executive overreach.

PiS also argued that by delegitimising a tribunal which had in the past ruled that the Polish Constitution superseded EU law, the Tusk government was paving the way for controversial social and economic policies to be pushed through without any domestic judicial oversight.

Tusk’s liberal critics

On the other hand, more ideologically supportive liberal critics of the Tusk government’s approach acknowledged the original 2015 irregularities but warned that selective non-recognition of an entire institution, combined with attempts to install a new tribunal without presidential participation, risked creating the same dual legitimacy problem that they accused PiS of having started.

They stressed that lasting repair required broad political consensus and careful adherence to formal procedures so that future majorities did not simply invert the non-recognition tactic. They noted the tension with earlier condemnations of PiS for elevating politically aligned figures or recently active politicians.

While sympathetic to the goal of reforming what they believed was a deeply compromised tribunal, these critics argued that, by employing legally questionable shortcuts and executive force, the Tusk government risked setting dangerous precedents and deepening the very disorder that it was claiming to correct.

Interestingly, the government’s broader “transitional justice” justificatory logic – that ordinary procedures would not adequately address a systemic capture and the priority had to be functional restoration rather than abstract purity – mirrored the arguments PiS itself advanced for its own judicial reforms after 2015.

The right-wing party argued that the post-1989 judiciary remained dominated by a post-communist elite that required deep structural overhaul rather than incremental change.

A high-risk escalation

The latest escalation is likely to entrench and intensify the profound systemic polarisation that characterises the Polish political scene, for a long-time embodied in the KO-PiS duopoly, with the conflict framed in existential terms of either “restoring the rule of law” or “defending the constitutional order”.

This fierce dispute lies at the heart of the Tusk government’s broader political “reckoning” (rozliczenie) agenda involving visibly removing PiS’s influence from key institutions.

For the ruling coalition, this was a central 2023 election campaign message, and being seen to deliver on it is an absolute political necessity to satisfy and mobilise its electoral base. A confrontational approach thus serves to consolidate the government’s support among these core voters, who have grown increasingly impatient and want to see decisive action.

However, the government’s strategy is fraught with political risk. High-stakes tactics risk uniting its right-wing opponents and alienating moderate voters increasingly exhausted by endless, hyper-partisan institutional confrontation, legal brinkmanship and the optics of police deployments around a key state body.

They provide the president and right-wing opposition with a powerful counternarrative of constitutional vandalism ahead of the next parliamentary election.

Escalation is also straining relations within the ruling coalition, especially among more conservative or legalistic coalition partners who believe that a more fundamental constitutional “reset” based on a cross-party settlement is required to break the impasse in the longer term.

The leader of one of the parties in Poland’s ruling coalition has proposed a “constitutional reset” to resolve the crisis around the country’s top court.

It would involve removing all current judges and choosing new ones in a more consensual process https://t.co/xDwpRUVHxG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 6, 2026

Internationally, although the EU political establishment remains supportive of the Tusk government’s actions, they invite uneasy scrutiny of the stability of Poland’s legal system and have drawn explicit criticism from the US embassy.

The reliance on a “transitional justice” framing that echoes PiS’s earlier justifications for systemic change, combined with the appointment to the tribunal of a recent minister despite prior criticisms of politicised nominations, also undercuts government claims of consistent principle and provides the right with a powerful narrative of hypocrisy.

Legal dualism

Ultimately, this bitter dispute has paved the way for a protracted and deeply destabilising “legal dualism” that could plague the Polish state for years to come, with a tribunal simultaneously legitimate and illegitimate depending on who holds power.

By treating the tribunal as an illegitimate entity when its nominees did not control it, the current government has established a precedent.

Even if it now appears to have secured a clear majority for its own nominees, a future right-wing government and sympathetic president will have every incentive to use the exact same playbook: treating the reconstituted tribunal as a captured instrument of the liberal establishment, and regarding it as no more legitimate than the Tusk government did the PiS-era one.

Consequently, the tribunal’s authority, and legal certainty in Poland more generally, have been further eroded, leaving the country without a widely accepted arbiter to resolve constitutional disputes. There are no immediate prospects for a durable resolution of this conflict.

Poland has among the lowest levels of gun ownership in Europe, though the number of firearms licences being issued has risen in recent years and some politicians have called for expanded access to guns. Saturday’s attack was carried out by a man who legally owned firearms.

On Saturday, 24-year-old Michał Oksiński drove through the historic city centre of Kraków, which was packed with tourists and locals, firing at random from his car.

He killed six people and injured over a dozen more. Later in the day, the bodies of the perpetrator’s parents and sister were found in his home, where they had been shot dead.

Oksiński’s rampage was brought to an end in a shootout with two police officers, which left all three with serious injuries. On Monday morning, the police announced that Oksiński had died in hospital. One of the police officers remains in what is described as “serious but stable” condition.

A collection of artefacts associated with the Vandals and dating back almost 2,000 years has been handed anonymously to a museum in eastern Poland.

The collection includes a sword, spear and javelin heads, shield components and spurs. Museum staff do not know who originally discovered the burial or exactly where it was located, leaving the circumstances of the find largely a mystery.

The Father Stanisław Staszic Museum in Hrubieszów announced in a Facebook post that the objects had been passed to them anonymously through an intermediary.

The items are in poor condition and will undergo urgent conservation, with the iron components of the weapons particularly vulnerable after centuries in the ground.

They were also exposed to high temperatures during a burial practice in which the deceased was burned along with their personal belongings. The museum says that the nature of the objects indicates that their owner held a high social position.

The most notable object is a sword preserved in three pieces, reflecting the Vandal practice of deliberately breaking or bending weapons and other grave artefacts as part of funeral rituals. The collection also contains two spearheads, both broken.

Other items include a shield boss with a spike, a shield grip, a fragment of a knife, a belt buckle and two spurs. Fragments of a bone comb and a bronze fibula, used to fasten a cloak, were also recovered.

 

The circumstances surrounding the discovery and recovery of the objects remain unknown, but the museum says that, according to the information it has received, the burial site was discovered in an agricultural field several years ago in the municipality of Werbkowice.

“We intend to verify the exact location through archaeological excavations, most likely next summer,” they added. “Based on the information we have gathered, there are strong indications that there may be more similar burials in the area that have been disturbed by agricultural work.”

The opportunity to recover the objects and transfer them to an appropriate institution arose only recently. The museum said that a local metal detectorist played a key role in arranging the transfer, acting as an intermediary in securing the artefacts.

The recovery of the artefacts follows another recent archaeological discovery in the same region. In August, the museum announced that a metal boss from a warrior’s shield dating to the second century was found at a scrap metal yard near Hrubieszów.

The Vandals were an ancient Germanic people believed to have reached the territories of present-day Poland around the 3rd or 2nd century BC.

They lived in the region for several centuries and are generally associated by researchers with the Przeworsk culture, which flourished across parts of present-day Poland during the Iron Age and Roman period.

Around the turn of the 4th and 5th centuries AD, amid the expansion of the Huns, they left Central Europe and moved westwards into the declining Roman Empire. As the Vandals left Central Europe, the Slavic population gradually moved into the region over the following centuries.

The leader of one of the parties in Poland’s ruling coalition has put forward plans for a “constitutional reset” that he hopes can resolve the crisis around the country’s top court.

The proposal, presented on Thursday by deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, head of the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), would remove all current judges on the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) and allow new judges to be chosen only with the approval of 60% of members of parliament and the president.

To take effect, the measure would require amending Poland’s constitution, something that has happened only twice since the document was adopted in 1997 and which also requires a three-fifths majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament.

Kosiniak-Kamysz’s announcement comes amid the fallout from events last Friday, when eight new judges elected to the TK this year by the government’s majority in parliament seized control of the court.

They announced that its chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, had been suspended for failing to fulfil his duties, including by refusing to allow most of those judges to take up their seats on the court.

Święczkowski denounced the takeover as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the tribunal’s remaining six judges, who, like him, were appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, which brought the TK under its political influence when it ruled from 2015 to 2023.

 

As well as pitting judges aligned with the national-conservative PiS, which is now the main opposition party, and the current more liberal government against one another, the dispute also centres around the legitimacy of certain judges.

The government points to the fact that PiS unlawfully appointed three judges to the TK in 2015. As a result, both Polish and European courts have found the tribunal in its current form to be illegitimate.

Meanwhile, Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of the eight judges appointed by the government’s parliamentary majority this year, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications.

The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”

But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d
