The standoff has led some NGOs and experts to call for a “constitutional reset”, whereby the TK would be reformed to make the process of selecting judges more consensual and less politicised.

Indeed, the current government even proposed legislation in 2024 that would have required new TK judges to be approved by a three-fifths parliamentary majority. The plans would also have removed unlawfully appointed judges from the PiS era and annulled rulings they were involved in.

That prompted the president at the time, Andrzej Duda, who was also aligned with PiS, to send the bills to the TK, which was still packed with PiS-era judges, for assessment. The tribunal rejected them as unconstitutional the following year.

Now, Kosiniak-Kamysz has proposed new legislation intended to resolve the issue. His solution would create a mechanism under which parliament, at the request of the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS), could declare the TK “permanently incapable of performing its duties”.

Such a status could only be declared with the support of a three-fifths majority of both houses of parliament – the Sejm and the Senate – combined. It would have to come at the request of the KRS because, says Kosiniak-Kamysz, the terms of judges cannot be shortened without the participation of other judges.

The process of appointing new TK judges would involve the speaker of the Sejm proposing candidates after obtaining the opinions of the heads of the Supreme Court and the Supreme Administrative Court – which are separate from the TK – as well as professional bodies representing legal professions.

The candidates proposed by the speaker would also have to receive the prior consent of the president. For a new TK judge to be approved, they would have to receive the support of three fifths of members of the Sejm and Senate combined.

Kosiniak-Kamysz emphasised, however, that the measure was intended as a “one-time” emergency tool. “Later, we will return to the method of selecting judges described today in the constitution, or a better one, if there is a majority for it.”

The current method of choosing new TK judges requires only the support of a majority in the Sejm. However, judges must then swear an oath “before the president”, an issue that has become a bone of contention this year.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Tue, 10 Nov 2026 19:00:59 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Poundland owner set to release £10m to retailer ahead of MP questioning https://www.cityam.com/poundland-owner-set-to-release-10m-to-retailer-ahead-of-mp-questioning/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 18:40:33 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2476092

Gordon Brothers, the US investment firm which owns the retail group, will unlock the funds held on Poundland’s balance sheet as the first in a series [...]]]>

The owner of Poundland has agreed to release around £10m of funding in order to pay the firm’s suppliers a day before its bosses are grilled by the government.

Gordon Brothers, the US investment firm which owns the retail group, will unlock the funds held on Poundland’s balance sheet as the first in a series of payments, City AM understands.

Gordon Brothers pledged earlier today to protect jobs at the embattled retailer after pressure from the business secretary and mounting political backlash over its handling of a sale process, a source told City AM.

The US investment firm met with Jonathan Reynolds this afternoon to discuss the future of the company and its 12,000 staff.

A source close to Reynolds said the minister had stressed the group “must do everything in [its] power to protect jobs and provide certainty for workers”.

Sky News first reported the news of the injection for Poundland.

The source said Reynolds “is pleased to have secured this commitment from Gordon Brothers in the meeting and will continue to hold the company to account and closely monitor developments.”

City AM revealed last week Poundland is on course for an £18m profit despite its owner pushing for a sale and claiming that the retailer remains “challenged and vulnerable”.

Industry sources said the release of funds is a “vital step” but warned it did not necessarily mean the discount retailer could avoid falling into administration as soon as this week, according to Sky News.

Little-known ‘frontrunner’ emerges

The move from Gordon Brothers comes after it was revealed on Monday that little-known investment firm, Xyra Group Holdings, emerged as a “frontrunner” to buy Poundland has called on Steve Smith, the retailer’s founder, to bolster its bid for the struggling firm.

The investment firm, founded by 23-year-old Manvedeep Singh, has asked Smith to lend support to their £12.5m bid to keep Poundland afloat as the discount retailer veers towards collapse.

Smith has had conversations with Xyra Group in recent days but does not plan to take part in any takeover efforts until a deal has been completed, it is understood.

]]> 2476092Rosie Harris-Davison Rosie Harris-Davison A Lange & Söhne’s Anthony de Haas on Seikos, regrets and Radar Love https://www.cityam.com/a-lange-sohne-anthony-de-haas-seikos-regrets-radar-love/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 18:04:36 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2476100

The world of watches is often buried beneath glossy PR scripts, corporate data sheets, and carefully rehearsed press events. Making Time is a chance to strip all that away by pulling up a chair with some of the industry’s most influential figures and passionate watch collectors, a chance to talk about the human reality of [...]]]>

The world of watches is often buried beneath glossy PR scripts, corporate data sheets, and carefully rehearsed press events. Making Time is a chance to strip all that away by pulling up a chair with some of the industry’s most influential figures and passionate watch collectors, a chance to talk about the human reality of collecting: the emotional side of the pursuit, the regrets, the hard choices and, above all, the passion.

I sat down with Anthony de Haas, director of product development at A Lange & Söhne, the man responsible for some of the most complex mechanical creations on earth. But behind the German precision lies the soul of an enthusiast who still remembers every gear in his very first proper watch.

What’s on the wrist of A Lange & Söhne’s product chief?

Andy Blackmore: So, what’s on your wrist today, and why?

Tony de Haas: I’m wearing a prototype of the Minute Repeater Perpetual, the novelty we launched last year. I’m wearing it because we are testing a new lubrication. It’s an honour, of course, to wear this piece. I’m wearing it for a couple of weeks, and every week we will take measurements and check the lubrication under the microscope. We’re continuously testing.

AB: How many watches do you own? Do you know off the top of your head or would you have to check?

TDH: I’m not a big watch collector – I think I have 10 or 11. Certainly not all A Lange watches. I have a Lange watch, Seikos, two Longines and an IWC from the early days when I worked there.

AB: What takes you longer: deciding on your shoes or your watch?

TDH: Shoes. Because for shoes I have to think, ‘Okay, what kind of suit or jeans or trousers do I put on?’ That takes more time, because I need to look at other stuff to combine. A watch is just like, boom! I am in an excellent position that I can’t go wrong with the watch I wear, of course.

His first watch: A Longines automatic

AB: What was the first proper watch you bought with your own money?

TDH: It was a Longines automatic. L919 calibre. It was a used watch from 1979, a double barrel, very nice, thin movement. I still have it.

AB: And I’ve still got my grandfather’s solid gold Longines. Is there a style of watch you actively avoid? Anything too flashy, dressy or trendy?

TDH: Yeah, I’m not a trendy guy. I’m more about timeless – I’ve been too long at A Lange & Söhne! I like the timelessness of the design. I’m not a fan of, ‘Oh wow, that’s cool! A watch with a green dial,’ or something like that. I think timelessness and quality is more important. Or emotion, you know? Memories. When I was 10, I got a Seiko 5 from my parents, an automatic, and I still have it. That’s an emotional thing.

AB: I know you said you’re not much of a watch collector, but would picking up a genuine classic for a song on eBay or in a flea market still give you a buzz?

TDH: No.

AB: Do you wear every watch you own, or are some too precious?

TDH: No, I wear everything I have.

AB: If the house is on fire, what single watch would you grab?

TDH: My Lange! That’s the only one. Or maybe the first Seiko from my parents.

AB: Is that your most precious watch?

TDH: Emotionally, yes.

The Longines that found its way back

AB: Is there a watch in your collection that has a personal story that’s got nothing to do with watchmaking?

TDH: I have one. I did watchmaking school in Holland, for four years. The first three years you do school, and then you do your exam, and then you have your internship in the last year. I went and worked at a watch shop with two watchmakers and three goldsmiths.

It was quite a big shop, with nice watches. They let me just go through the drawers and everything to find my way around. And in a rack I saw a really damaged Longines. The glass was gone, the dial was scratched, and there was rust in the movement.

The owner said, ‘You know what? That’s a nice project for you. You restore that watch, and then we sell it. Learn how to polish the case, redo everything, order the parts…’ So I restored the watch, and I really loved it. When I finished it, he said I’d done an excellent job and he put it in the shop window. I wanted to buy it but I couldn’t afford it. Two days later, he said, ‘Congratulations, I sold the watch’.

About 10 months later, on the last day of my apprenticeship, they gave me that watch as a leaving gift! That made me so happy. Of course I still own it today – so I have two Longines.

Regrets, quartz and IWC Porsche Design

AB: Is there a watch you regret buying?

TDH: Hm. Not really. I’m a big fan of the IWC Porsche Design watches from the 80s and 90s, the titanium ones. I considered buying one but I thought, you know what, I’m not going to wear it so why should I have it? If I buy a watch, I need to wear it. I’m not going to buy it to put it in a safe.

AB: Is there anything you regret selling?

TDH: No, because I never sold one.

AB: An easy one, then! How do you feel about quartz watches?

TDH: Great! I repaired them. I worked six years at Seiko Netherlands in the after-sales department, so I did a lot of quartz. I did the old 7A’s, I did the ultra-thin Lassale’s with the very thin movements. Seiko is a great high-tech company.

AB: Do you ever spot someone’s watch and stop them to ask more?

TDH: I met someone wearing a special edition of the Ocean 2000 Porsche Design IWC diver, one that was made for the German navy. They had a black bezel and a red hand. I used to repair them! I stopped them to say ‘That’s a very special watch’.

Life at A Lange & Söhne

AB: Do you ever worry you take watches too seriously?

TDH: No. I don’t take myself too seriously. I have a team of technicians, engineers and movement designers who have the day-to-day struggles of finding solutions for problems – there is enough seriousness in the company. But humour can be a good way to find solutions.

On the bumpy road of developing a watch, you have problems. And that’s cool because you get to solve them. It’s fun! You have a dream, and you try to reach that dream. If you start moaning, you don’t find a solution.

AB: How does your other half feel about your relationship with watches?

TDH: Sometimes she says, ‘Okay, you have two daughters, you have me, but Lange is your baby.’ And it is a bit true. It’s always been like that. Today it’s better because my daughters are aged 24 and 26, so they have their own thing now. But work-life balance has been a struggle sometimes. Having said that, I’ve never been the guy who works from 7am until 10pm. When I wasn’t travelling, I would be home for dinner.

But there is an internal conflict, you know? I’m a person who lives intensely. I’m an emotional, intense guy.

AB: Have you ever thought that in some ways you are immortal, because the watches you have created will be here long after we’ve gone?

TDH: No, I don’t think so much about that, although it is probably true. But I don’t take myself that seriously. Especially in the world we live in today, where the craziest things are happening. It would be good for the world if more people would take themselves less seriously. What we do at A Lange & Söhne is not only me. I’m just one part of the puzzle. But you need all the pieces for the puzzle to work.

Radar Love: The drumming watchmaker

AB: One last question! I know you’re a keen drummer and that you were taught to play by Cesar Zuiderwijk from Golden Earring. Would you swap everything you’ve achieved to play the drums on their biggest hit Radar Love?

TDH: No, because I already did play the drums on Radar Love! It was on a Dutch television show, 33 years ago. I have it on my Instagram!

CHELTENHAM’s three-day November Meeting begins on Friday with several big guns of the Jumps scene set to emerge.

Jonbon is slated to return in Friday’s Grade Two Shloer Chase (2.20pm) in a bid to win the contest for a third time and looks to have every chance once again.

However, there are more enticing ante-post opportunities on Saturday with the big betting race of the meeting being the Paddy Power Gold Cup (2.20pm).

A winner at the Festival in March, Meetmebythesea makes his anticipated reappearance, and with such a good record when fresh and at Cheltenham, he could be tough to beat.

At 3/1 he’s short enough though, and I’d rather play a couple against him in a race that could cut up on account of the lack of rain.

With the going at Prestbury Park currently described as good and not much rain in the forecast before the weekend, conditions should remain quick for the time of year.

ZURICH is one horse that should relish the ground.

Irish raiders don’t have a great record in this race, but I think Henry de Bromhead could set that record straight this year.

It’s often important to have had a run prior to arriving at this race, and this seven-year-oldappeals as a type that has been targeted at the contest.

He returned last month when finishing fifth over just shy of this trip at Limerick and that run should have left him spot on for this assignment.

He ran a big race in the Plate at the Festival in March, finishing fifth behind Madara, which was a fine effort considering he was badly impeded at the first fence.

With a win over this course and distance last October on good ground already to his name, we know he handles conditions and the demands of Cheltenham well.

He’s now eight pounds better off at the weights with Madara, and after only 13 starts, there should be more to come from him.

At 12/1 in places, he’s well worth an each-way play.

I’m also keen to have a 12/1 each-way saver on De Bromhead’s other runner, JULY FLOWER, who judging by recent stable tour comments has also been aimed at this prize.

This mare won the Grade Two Arkle Trial at last year’s November Meeting, so also has good course form to her name.

That win came on her seasonal reappearance, meaning coming here without a run is not really a concern.

She ran some fine races in Grade One company last season, including when third behind Romeo Coolio at Leopardstown, where she was only half-a-length behind recent Kopek Des Bordes conqueror Irish Panther.

That sort of form suggests she is well treated off a mark of just 142.

She has won over this trip in the past and, while she might benefit from a bit more of an ease in the ground, having won on good-to-yielding in the past, conditions should be manageable for her.

In the following three-mile handicap hurdle (2.55pm) on Saturday, GOLD FOR ALEC makes plenty of appeal at 6/1.

Tom Symonds’ six-year-old arrives here fit and in good form after two runs so far this season.

He was in the process of running a big race when crashing out at the last at Chepstow on reappearance, and proved himself no worse for that experience when a fine second over this course and distance last month.

In all likelihood, he bumped into a well-handicapped horse that day in Seaniecon, and while he has been put up three pounds for that effort, another big run looks on the cards.

July Flower e/w                               2.20pm               Cheltenham

Gold For Alec e/w                          2.55pm               Cheltenham

]]> 2475963Ed Culham Ed Culham 2mins: The startup tackling Britain’s financial literacy crisis https://www.cityam.com/2mins-startup-financial-literacy-crisis/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 17:00:50 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2476069

Father-daughter duo Chris and Emily Boxall are using microlearning and gamification to tackle the UK's financial knowledge crisis via their app, 2mins]]>

The UK has one of the lowest levels of financial literacy in the developed world. A 2024 Santander study found that only 47 per cent of UK adults could correctly answer at least five out of seven financial knowledge questions, compared with 62 per cent across OECD countries. The same survey found that only 1 per cent of primary school teachers believed their pupils had adequate financial skills.

The government is expanding financial literacy through curriculum mandates and the HM Treasury’s Financial Inclusion Strategy, under which financial education will become statutory in primary schools across England starting in Autumn 2028. But critics argue this will still leave millions of children each year woefully unprepared for real life.

That challenge inspired Emily Boxall and her father, Chris, to set up their edTech startup 2mins to try and address this growing problem.

The genesis of the idea came from Chris’s interactions with clients at Fundamental Asset Management, many of whom were wealthy, sophisticated investors who simply valued plain-English clarity over industry jargon. “I think it was at this point that I realised that I could bring something”, says Emily. “I felt like I could bring the solution because I’ve got this different way of thinking about things,” she adds.

The team ended up creating 2mins, an app designed to teach users about money through a series of original, engaging, and challenging games. Since launching in January, 2mins has attracted over 2,000 users, who compete against each other to rack up the highest scores by playing a series of games every week. Games are designed, as the name suggests, to be played in 2mins, a name and format chosen to remove some of the stigma associated with financial education. Emily has taken on the role of chief games creator, developing the idea of each game and then putting that idea into practice with the help of AI.

Initially, Emily says they received critical feedback about the nature of the games and, in particular, the animals. “I asked if we needed to change it to fit all the feedback?” Emily explained. “But we said no; we’re doing this to be different, to be bold, and we’re trying to reach people who haven’t been reached before by this. And we stuck with it. And I’m so glad that we have.”

2mins: A tool for schools

Now being piloted in nine schools across the UK, 2mins aims to make financial education easier for teachers to deliver and more engaging for students. While the government has taken important steps to put financial education on the curriculum, there’s still a lot to do. And telling schools to do something doesn’t necessarily mean they will.

Schools and teachers are constrained by time and resources. That’s where Emily and Chris believe they have an edge. “When schools need to deliver financial education as part of the curriculum, hopefully they’ll look to 2mins as a really accessible, easy way to deliver that education”, Emily explains.

While schools are a key focus of its current expansion, 2mins was originally designed for users aged 16 and over and has also attracted an enthusiastic adult following. “We’ve got a lovely group of over 45-year-old women playing,” says Emily, highlighting one example. The next version of the app will also be designed with teachers in mind, following lessons learned during the testing phase.

“It is about trying to engage the teacher; I think that’s the hardest part; it’s less about the student, more about the teacher,” Chris explains. “That’s probably the hardest thing that was a bit of an unknown,” he adds.

The corporate market

The father-daughter team are also developing the app for a rather different market: corporate HR departments.

The business is currently in discussions with a major corporate client to develop an app for new starters and younger employees, helping them navigate incentives and benefits on offer, from pension entitlement to share schemes and even parental leave.

The corporate version will build on the same principles as the original app, with bespoke content and branding designed around each company’s employee benefits, culture and objectives. The aim is to create something that’s “fun and light-hearted” that the company’s employees still want to engage with. “The last thing users want is to be lectured or educated in the formal sense,” Chris says.

Creating products for this market, Chris says, was always a long-term goal once 2mins proved itself with the most demanding audience: young people.

Following the completion of its initial schools pilot, Emily and Chris plan to roll out an enhanced version of 2mins in 2027, initially targeting independent schools with a paid subscription model and a dedicated teacher dashboard. At the same time, they want to continue developing the corporate product to cultivate this potentially lucrative market and attract a sponsor to help fund the rollout across state schools.

By combining gamification with accessible microlearning, 2mins is working to transform financial literacy for pupils and employees alike. Its success was recognised earlier this year when 2mins was awarded the runner-up award at The Money Awareness and Inclusion Awards for Best Fintech/AI by a For Profit Organisation, and the winner of Best Content Creation at the Financial Capability Awards.

As the app moves toward nationwide expansion, Emily and Chris Boxall’s innovative approach offers a promising solution to bridge the UK’s financial knowledge gap and empower the next generation.

]]> 2476069Rupert Hargreaves Rupert Hargreaves Will Polymarket and Kalshi ever lead prediction market surge in UK? https://www.cityam.com/will-polymarket-and-kalshi-ever-lead-prediction-market-surge-in-uk/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 17:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2475871

Around $2bn was staked on prediction markets across last week’s US midterm elections, yet sites like Polymarket and Kalshi aren’t categorised as bookmakers across the pond. The sector is rapidly growing, with binary markets becoming subject to increased spend across America: how many tweets Elon Musk will post on X today is a real market, [...]]]>

Around $2bn was staked on prediction markets across last week’s US midterm elections, yet sites like Polymarket and Kalshi aren’t categorised as bookmakers across the pond.

The sector is rapidly growing, with binary markets becoming subject to increased spend across America: how many tweets Elon Musk will post on X today is a real market, alongside the next Democratic presidential nominee, the price of Bitcoin at 6am tomorrow morning and what Anthropic’s IPO closing market cap will be.

It has led to a number of contracts across American sport, with a deal between Major League Baseball and Polymarket potentially worth over £200m. The NBA last month got on the bandwagon, announcing partnerships with both Kalshi and Polymarket. So are they coming to the Premier League, Hundred or other UK competitions? 

The reality is that prediction markets would need to penetrate a very mature betting market to operate in the UK. From a scratchcard at 16 to a bingo hall at 86 – and everything in between – the British betting market is already varied and very closely regulated. The closest thing the UK has to a prediction market lever – betting exchanges like Betfair – are monitored by the Gambling Commission.

Combined with oversight from the Financial Conduct Authority and the costs associated with obtaining a licence to operate here, it is more likely that prediction markets would follow the playbook of Asian betting sites, which are inaccessible to Brits but have spent big on UK sponsorships with global reach, such as Premier League football clubs.

Regulation on the way?

“Regulation is the significant barrier for entry, rather than any demand concern,” sport finance expert Professor Rob Wilson tells City AM. “The US markets see them positioned as a type of financial exchange whereas the UK indicates they’re more like gambling operators hence the licensing requirement.

London's centuries-old cigar trade and thriving lounge scene make it the world's best city for hand-rolled cigar smokers, says The Emory's head of cigars, Blue Curran.]]>

London is, without a doubt, the best city in the world for hand-rolled cigar smokers, explains Blue Curran, head of cigars at The Emory Cigar Merchants.

The city’s edge lies in its history. Smokers have bought, sold, imported and exported cigars from London for centuries, and that means the capital has one of the biggest reserves of cigars anywhere in the world.

London’s cigar debut occurred in 1814, when British officers returned from the Peninsular War carrying gifts from their Spanish comrades. The product was snapped up by Britain’s smokers in the thousands of tobacco houses, private clubs and pubs across the country. The first cigar manufacturer in London was William Kelly and Sons, which opened in 1870, and over the following years the industry continued to put down roots in the capital.

In the 20th Century, names such as Alfred Dunhill and Davidoff of London opened their doors, joining Robert Lewis, founded in 1787 on St James’s Street, which later counted Sir Winston Churchill and Oscar Wilde among its customers. In 1992, it joined forces with James J. Fox. Sautter of Mount Street also joined the collection.

Most of these names still have a presence in the city despite policymakers’ attempts to clamp down on smoking. There’s also a thriving cigar lounge scene, with locations such as The Emory Cigar Merchants, The Connaught Cigar Merchants and the Garden Room at the Lanesborough Hotel on Hyde Park Corner.

Although smoking indoors is generally illegal in the UK, the law permits dedicated, specialist cigar shops to have an indoor tasting or sampling room where customers can smoke cigars or pipe tobacco. That’s why rooms like those found in The Emory are technically classed as cigar shops.

The life of a hand-rolled cigar

Outsiders and non-smokers often lump cigarettes and cigars into the same category, but as Blue explains, they could not be more different.

Hand-rolled cigars make up four per cent of the global cigar market by volume, but nearly a third of the overall market value. Machine-manufactured cigars make up the remainder. Unlike the mass-produced machine-made cigars, it can take years to learn the art of cigar rolling, and many days to roll an individual cigar.

Cuba is the spiritual home of the cigar, but due to export restrictions and output limitations, the market today is dominated by other Central American countries such as Ecuador and Nicaragua, as well as the Dominican Republic.

The most common hand-rolled cigar size is the so-called Robusto size. A short, thick cigar that measures roughly 5 inches in length with a 50 ring gauge (typically ranging from 4.75 to 5.5 inches long and 48 to 52 ring gauge). These can take five years to grow and roll with care, going through every stage of the growing and production process. Each cigar contains at least four different tobacco leaves: a binder leaf to hold it all together and a wrapper leaf on top.

These are vital to the cigar’s taste and curated for the perfect look and feel and are the largest type of leaf you’ll find in a cigar. Selected for size, colour and a lack of imperfections, these leaves are often grown under canopies, such as cheesecloth, that diffuse direct sunlight and alter how the plant grows. This ultimately makes the leaves stretchier, smoother and thinner.

Ultimately, each cigar has a unique taste and flavour. When stored properly in a controlled environment (typically around 65 per cent to 70 per cent relative humidity and 18°C to 21°C), cigars can last for decades, or even a century. Older cigars lose some of their harshness, replaced by sweetness or peppiness, but strength isn’t consistent from brand to brand.

While the Robusto is the most common, other sizes, such as the Churchill (7 inches long with a ring gauge of 47) are perhaps more associated with the category. The Churchill, named after Sir Winston, an avid cigar smoker, was previously known as a Large Corona, the larger version of the Corona, the benchmark size (5 1/2 to 6 inches) against which all other cigars are measured. Longer, fatter cigars burn at a lower temperature and last much longer than shorter, thinner cigars.

Cigar smoking in London: how to enjoy it

“It’s the time and effort that’s gone into the cigar” that makes smoking each one such a special experience, explains Blue. They are not designed to be smoked in a hurry. Cigars are designed to be enjoyed and smoked with friends. They’re meant to pass the time in a friendly way, he adds. “Smoke it how you want,” Blue explains. As long as you are enjoying the experience, don’t let anyone tell you any different.

“One of the big things about cigar smoking is not coming away smelling of cigars,” explains Blue. That’s a mark of a good cigar lounge, he adds – you should be able to leave after enjoying your time and not carry the smell around.

Each one of London’s cigar bars and lounges has created its own collection of cigars. These are usually curated by the venue or its dedicated head of cigars, and each collector leaves their unique stamp on the collection. As Blue explains, some collectors prefer older, more unique cigars, which they spend their time scouring the market for. Others may take a more relaxed approach to curation.

Another reason London has carved out a unique place for cigar smokers and collectors.

There’s a snobbishness that persists about Val Thorens. There’s the view that it’s “soulless” because it’s a comparatively new resort, having opened in 1971. But actually that was so long ago now that the first people born here are facing retirement.

One of these people is Aurélie Rey, the daughter of one of the founders of the resort, who runs the Alpen Art restaurant in the centre of town. Look Rey in the eyes and tell her that her food is “soulless” and you’ll see what a ridiculous notion this is.

Place Caron: The best people watching in the Alps

Also not soulless: Val Thorens’ main square Place Caron, where skiers heading to the slopes converge. I become obsessed with watching the goings on here over morning coffee from my prime position on my slopeside balcony at Hôtel Le Fitz Roy. It’s not breaking news to suggest town squares are good for people watching, although Place Caron is particularly vibey, even for ski resorts.

Two scenes converge in Val Thorens, at Europe’s highest ski resort. There are those with money who like the fancy but not ridiculously fancy collection of four and five-star hotels, and the young party types who come for the frankly overwhelming opportunity to ski in any direction you like, the music festivals and the nightlife.

Actually, there’s another set too. The vibe is so potent here that lots of people appear to have no interest in skiing at all. And not in the Courchevel ‘I’m spending a day shopping at Gucci’ way, more that this is just a functioning, authentic, lively town, that just so happens to be ear-bleedingly high.

The type of person who goes to Val Thorens is my type of human: into the finer things but not a dick about it. I watch every walk of life collide at Place Caron. An octogenarian couple from Monaco turning redder and redder as they squint below the sun at the gulf of mountains; a group of British lads bringing the tone down; and punctual Scandinavians frustrated by all the hubbub. They just want to ski past and get on (in their colourful ski suits they look like the fragmented colour flashes of a hologram). Unless you’re a thorough misery, or Parisian, this hodge-podge of French, Brits, Dutch, Scandinavians and, more recently, Americans means you don’t have to look far for conversation.

Why Val Thorens is the world’s best ski resort

How else should I talk about how great Val Thorens is? How about the kilometres of slopes that suit every type of skier, the near-guaranteed snow (we’re at a squiffy 2,300 metres), and direct connection to Les 3 Vallées, the largest ski area in the world, accessible via one pass?

Val Thorens has won world’s best ski resort for the tenth year out of thirteen at the World Ski Awards, voted for by the public and ski tourism professionals. That accolade drew me in the first place, helping me decide from dozens of similar-sounding places in the Alps that can feel hard to distinguish between.

Where to stay in Val Thorens: Hôtel Le Fitz Roy

Hôtel Le Fitz Roy is exactly the Val Thorens ticket: fancy but not stifling, it is a handsome slopeside property with all of the functional necessities, such as ski-in ski-out access, good local food, a nice spa, and a terrace on Place Caron, on which I spent more time than I’d like to admit surveying the action (yes, I skied a bit, but who wants those boots on for more than four hours a day?).

Vintage resort photos adorn the walls of the common areas, which are lovely and cozy and draw you in for late-afternoon board games, although I often ended up in the underground spa. Rooms are spacious and many have slopeside views, although the ones with the views up the mountain are fine too.

A highlight is meat straight from the al fresco winter barbecue, cooked by a man who makes it look perfectly ordinary to be barbecuing outdoors in sub-zero temperatures (it was boiling sunshine for most of our trip, which is common given the resort is often above the cloud line).

Caron 3200: The highest restaurant in Les 3 Vallées

We ascend nearly another thousand metres by cable car for our second most memorable meal, though no one is suffering in silence this time. The mountaintop Caron 3200 restaurant, opened just over a year ago, is the highest restaurant in Les 3 Vallées, with spectacular views that feel as if from a plane’s window. We peer down at the clouds and the spread of mountains into Italy and France from the wine bar. There, we have lunch, in the form of an enormous meat and cheese board. We prefer this to the restaurant which, although nice, is fuller – we had the wine bar to ourselves. Order the rest of the bottle and sack off the afternoon’s ski plans to gawp out at this for a few hours. I’d imagine the equally fancy Ice Q, formerly the highest restaurant in Austria and used in the James Bond film Spectre, is fuming.

Val Thorens nightlife: Pints, fondue and cover bands

In search of anything that might be called soulless, that night we shake off our boots and wander into town, past local markets and the O’Connell’s Irish pub and The Frog & Roastbeef rock bar where we lived up to the Brits abroad cliche by sinking altogether too many pints.

Here, Americans – there are a lot of them, as skiing prices Stateside rocket – seem to be enjoying the British cover bands playing Oasis and Blur tracks more than the rest of us, who can bear this type of place for an hour but are drawn to the exit by the inevitable opening chords for Wonderwall. Opposite more obviously touristic restaurants, including a themed Latin American restaurant called Favela, is La Chaumière, a quietly brilliant French restaurant with polished wooden walls and bench seating, where we enjoyed fondue.

In fact, Val Thorens is chocca with homely places to linger over; for a week there is equal amount of authenticity and heart here as in the more historical Alpine destinations.

Le Rooftop is another, where waitstaff are just the warmest and the food is generous: duck, great cuts of meat and more fondue. If you want to amp it up, swerve the more clublike apres ski and go for the ostentatious but not overly so La Maison, another of the resort’s oldest restaurants, with its iconic redback chairs and prime slopeside view, where the cocktails are good.

La Folie Douce: The Alps’ most famous party

If you want more of the boots-on-table British image of a French ski holiday, La Folie Douce on the Plein Sud run – a blue run, suitable for most skiers – is one of the Alps’ most lauded party spots. La Fruitière is the chic restaurant here: book lunch and pre-game ahead of a dance on the main bar floor, which becomes truly ridiculous by mid-afternoon. Expect champagne pourings, live singers (who stand out half naked in any weather, including blizzards), live saxophonists, dancers, and hundreds of wasted people dancing to electronic music on the tabletops.

For plenty more options, the main snow front of Rond Point des Pistes has more of this type of nonsense, plus sophisticated restaurants, and runs pretty much the length of the town.

Is Val Thorens worth it?

Other places do other things better: sports professionals love Val d’Isere for its no-nonsense ski focus; Meribel, with its treelines and stone-built 1900s restaurants, brings the proper history. But forget box-ticking and go for an all-round vibe at Val Thorens.

Why do we get our knickers in such a twist for truffles – and the white truffle above all? The Greeks and Romans loved them; the Egyptians ate them dipped in goose fat and the Catholic church described them as sinful.

Why do they cost so much?

Given these little fungi’s stubborn inability to be farmed or mass produced, there is a limited supply, which, given their short shelf life, drives prices sky high. They are aphrodisiacs, not just because you’re flashing the cash to potential partners but also because – so the story goes – their musky scent triggers subconscious feelings of attraction and comfort in some humans (and curiously, most female pigs).

When is white truffle season?

The black truffle is present in different forms across the year but right now we have hit white truffle season, which runs until December and means we get to eat one of the most expensive ingredients to be found.

As my invitation to the Alba white truffle fair in Italy’s Piedmont got lost in the post, I did the next best thing and went for lunch at Bocconcino Mayfair.

The best wine for white truffle: Nebbiolo

You’ll have spent a hefty amount on this little lump of gold so it would be remiss to order anything that might reduce its pleasure. The best wine for white truffle is a Nebbiolo, a grape that comes from the same region, Piedmont. It’s a pale, ethereal red, tricking the unknowing drinker into thinking it is light in the mouth, but it has taut, fine-boned tannins and layers of dusky flavours from cherry to violets and, almost always, this mushroomy, truffly note. Barolo and Barbaresco are the premium versions, named respectively the “King” and “Queen” of wines. Barolo is aged longer and is structured, powerful and dense with flavour, whereas Barbaresco comes generally from lower slopes and is typically softer. Both are superb and premium.

If you are looking to snaffle a bargain, then hunt out a Langhe Nebbiolo, which delivers absolute beauty in the glass but at a much more approachable price.

Eating white truffle at Bocconcino Mayfair

I drank through a bottle of Langhe Nebbiolo at Bocconcino and it was a joy with their thin, flavourful slivers of beef carpaccio topped with shavings of creamy white truffle, followed by an excellent white risotto, similarly decked out. The table became engulfed in a cloud of truffle perfume. Given their fragility, speed and skill are required and the truffles I was eating at lunch were harvested in Italy only the morning before. So, order the Nebbiolo (or if you prefer a white, then an elegantly oaked chardonnay) and indulge in this brief window of opportunity for one of nature’s greatest delicacies.

The trailblazing leader was “somebody who would speak about free markets, free enterprise, the rule of law, a woman being a prime minister”.

This year’s Booker Prize winner feels less like high literature and more like a collective nervous breakdown, writes Harry Owen

Gather together five unconventional judges, hand them 163 novels to whittle down to one Booker Prize winner, and you should expect a peculiar outcome. This year’s judging panel reads like an eccentric, avant-garde dinner party. Chaired by Cambridge classicist Mary Beard and flanked by Pulp front-man Jarvis Cocker, the rest of the band’s lineup includes online-surrealist poet Patricia Lockwood, ‘lyrical innovator’ Raymond Antrobus and cultural critic Rebecca Liu. A ‘challenging’ winner was inevitable, but The End of Everything by M. John Harrison is totally bonkers.

I read dystopia – it’s my genre – but this was too weird even for me. Set in a decaying Britain where London has been abandoned and the surviving population huddles in squalid tented cities along the South Coast, the narrative drifts across a wasteland strewn with crashed airliners and rusted shipping containers. At the heart of it is an elderly, rifle-toting aunt steadily succumbing to dementia, accompanied by a bewildered nephew trying to navigate the ruins. 

At least for the first few chapters this is what’s happening. However, lurking on the shoreline is the bizarre ‘iGhetti’, a sentient beach-blob that steadily swells in size, absorbs coastal debris and begins telepathically bossing the surviving humans around.

A winner for the stockpiling age?

I can see why the judges fell for it. Beard would relish the themes of collapsing empires, while Cocker was bound to harbour affection for that distinctly grubby, rain-soaked English seaside melancholy. Harrison certainly creates an unforgettable atmosphere, the mood throughout is like a vivid fever dream – this element gets top marks.

The age-old question of whether art reflects life or vice versa feels particularly apt this year. I literally find myself stockpiling instant noodles, baked beans and wind-up radios, so parts of The End of Everything undeniably strike a nerve. Yet as the world around us slowly goes sideways, did we really need Britain’s highest fiction honour handed to a blob-slime barking orders on a pebble beach?? The oddest jury in recent memory gave us a book that feels less like high literature and more like a collective nervous breakdown – maybe that’s what we deserve.

If you’re considering reading it, my advice is simple – don’t bother. Pick up Exit Party by Emily St. John Mandel instead. It’s a brilliant companion to Station Eleven, a dystopian novel that feels just recognisable enough to hit home, without pushing you over the edge of sanity. Or take our lifestyle editor Steve Dineen’s advice and try Black Bag, another Booker nominee with an admittedly absurd blob-based premise – a lecturer pays a man to attend his classes dressed with a black bag over his head and body, just his legs sticking out the bottom – which he called a “hell of a read” nonetheless.

The Post Office has agreed to end a contract it has held with Fujitsu for over 25 years and hand over operations to Accenture by next year.

It was confirmed on Tuesday the three organisations had jointly agreed that Accenture would take control of its IT systems sometime between 1 June and 1 September 2027, with the final date due to be confirmed in March 2027.

The Post Office has held the contract with Fujitsu since 1999.

The Japanese tech company was the heart of the Post Office Horizon scandal in which its flawed Horizon software caused a series of financial shortfalls in sub-postmasters’ branch accounts. More than 900 sub-postmasters were wrongfully convicted between 1999 and 2015, which led to the Post Office Inquiry.

The Post Office paid £95m to Fujitsu in 2024 to extend the contract for two years, after a plan to move to Amazon was ditched, according to reports.

The Post Office said it will be a “handover process that will ensure continuity and operational stability for customers and postmasters whilst the Horizon system is transferred to Accenture from Fujitsu.”

The Post Office’s current contract with Fujitsu runs until March 2027. The firm confirmed a “short, time-limited contract extension has also been agreed to facilitate the transition process.”

The Post Office said it will retire Horizon from its operations as part of it’s five-year transformation plan which “will see software and hardware throughout the historic institution upgraded to meet the needs of the modern customer with greater flexibility and convenience.”

Chief executive of the Post Office, Neil Brocklehurst announced in May 2026 that Accenture would be undertaking a ‘walk in and take over’ exercise for the current Horizon system, assuming day to day operations from Fujitsu, as well as developing the back-end of the new system to replace Horizon which will be used in branches.

Alongside Accenture, the new system will be developed in partnership with tech suppliers OneView Commerce and Escher, which the post office said it will “work closely” with to “introduce a simpler and more effective IT system throughout the branch network.”

“Ending our contract with Fujitsu is a critical milestone in Post Office’s transformation, and today’s agreement secures the transition away from Fujitsu and over to Accenture safely and responsibly to achieve our target of summer 2027,” Brocklehurst said.

The chief executive added the firm is “working at pace” with Accenture, Oneview Commerce and Escher “to build a modern, resilient platform able to make everyday life easier for customers and postmasters for years to come.”

Matt Prebble, head of Accenture in the UK & Ireland, said: “We understand how important it is that postmasters can continue serving their customers and communities throughout this transformation. Our priority is a safe and carefully managed transition that supports continued trading in branches.” 

Barristers charged with misconduct

The end of the contract comes after two of the solicitors in relation to the Horizon IT scandal were referred to The Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal in June and charged with misconduct.

The regulator confirmed it was taking action against Jane MacLeod, the former Post Office general counsel from 2015 to 2019, and Nick Gould, a partner who represented former sub-postmistress Seema Misra to overturn her conviction in 2021. It is alleged Gould failed to provide adequate information in relation to legal costs and the scope of the legal work to clients he was representing, including Misra.

In October, during a case management hearing, MacLeod was accused by the SRA of “putting her own convenience” first by filing an application to appear remotely from Australia for a Tribunal hearing over alleged misconduct during the Horizon IT Scandal.

A Bank of England rate-setter has warned the UK jobs market is “stuck in low gear” as young people risk “lasting scars” from employers retreating on hiring.

Claire Lombardelli, deputy governor for monetary policy at the central bank, told a City conference that the labour market was cooling “mainly through less hiring rather than more firing”.

While economic activity had proven “unexpectedly robust”, she cautioned the pattern in the labour market posed a brewing issue.

“A low-hire, low-fire labour market creates its own problems. It protects those already in work while making it much harder for those trying to get in or move on,” she said.

“The labour market has become less effective at moving people towards new opportunities. The labour market is stuck in low gear.”

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said vacancy levels had decreased to the lowest since April 2021 in September at 691,000. This came despite the unemployment rate falling to 4.7 per cent, its lowest since July last year.

Lombardelli said the labour market could “preserve existing jobs while dropping down a gear under the bonnet”.

She warned that the costs of the hiring freeze are “falling particularly heavily on young people, for whom the first step into work has become harder”. The youth unemployment rate for those aged between 16 and 24 was surged to 16.4 per cent in the three months to July, reaching an 11-year-high.

Bank of England: Minimum wage driving youth unemployment

Lombardelli said young people now account for around 40 per cent of all unemployment and warned joblessness early in working life “leaves lasting scars on employment and earnings.”

“Missing the first steps on the job ladder delays the accumulation of skills and experience,” she said, warning that “a cyclical shortage of entry-level jobs can therefore become a structural loss of productive capacity.”

She pointed to recent increases in minimum wage as dampening demand. Labour’s manifesto promised to remove “discriminatory” minimum wage bands for young people and bring wages in line with the living wage by 2030.

But the growing jobs crisis for young people has triggered a rethink of the policy. Chancellor John Healey hiked the minimum wage by 3.9 per cent at the Budget, setting the floor for wages for over-21s at £13.20 for the coming year, while the rate for younger workers was raised by an equal 3.9 per cent to £11.27.

Healey told the BBC after the Budget that the Treasury would take equalising the rates “one step at a time” following concerns that larger rises could exacerbate youth unemployment.

Lombardelli said that for young workers, “the greater barrier may not be cost alone, but perceived risk.”

“For an employer, taking on a young person involves uncertainty and investment. New entrants need training, supervision and we hear increasingly about work readiness and the need for pastoral support,” she explained.

“When firms face uncertainty, the risk of inaction in terms of pausing hiring new workers is often less than the risk of letting experienced employees go. That asymmetry has contributed to lower hiring of young people.”

On interest rates the deputy governor said there was “likely to be a case” for another rate hike in the “near term” after a lack of evidence for weaker inflation pressures.

The Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee unanimously voted to increase interest rates to four per cent in its meeting earlier this month.

The world’s most valuable chipmaker shed around $190bn (£145bn) in market value on Monday after chief executive Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence, triggering an FBI investigation and a shareholder lawsuit.

Jason Hollands, managing director at Evelyn Partners’ Bestinvest, warned that the fallout could reach British savers who have never directly invested in Nvidia.

“The wider question for investors is whether their overall portfolio is too dependent on a small number of large technology companies,” he told City AM.

“For every £100 invested in an S&P 500 Index fund, Nvidia currently represents around £7.”

The warning exposes the extent to which British retirement savings have become tied to America’s AI boom.

Around 45 per cent of assets held in British pension schemes are invested in US shares, according to investment bank Panmure Liberum, leaving savers exposed to Wall Street’s biggest technology companies.

Nvidia alone accounts for around seven per cent of the S&P 500, while the growing popularity of passive investing means millions of Britons hold indirect stakes through workplace pensions, stocks and shares ISAs and global tracker funds.

Even funds marketed as globally diversified can be heavily weighted towards American technology companies, with the US accounting for well over half of the MSCI World Index.

“A tracker may hold hundreds of companies, but market-cap weighting can still leave it concentrated in a handful of names,” Hollands said.

The risks are particularly acute for defined contribution pension holders, whose retirement savings fluctuate with financial markets, rather than defined benefit members receiving a guaranteed retirement income.

Nvidia shares closed 4.3 per cent lower on Monday, despite the Nasdaq 100 rallying 3.4 per cent, as investors weighed the potential implications for Huang’s leadership.

The complaint, brought by investor Mark Kistenmacher, accuses the company of misleading shareholders by failing to disclose Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data centre operator Megaspeed.

US authorities reportedly suspect Alice Huang of links to Chinese intelligence, allegations Beijing has rejected.

Huang apologised to employees on Sunday for being unfaithful to his wife, while Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

Donald Trump subsequently confirmed that the FBI was examining the matter, although he defended Huang after speaking to him personally.

Nvidia’s board said it had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security had been compromised and expressed confidence in its chief executive.

“What matters is whether shareholders have suffered loss due to Nvidia failing to disclose material information, particularly given the sensitivities surrounding China, AI chips and US export controls,” Lorraine Lanceley, partner in commercial and securities litigation at Stewarts, told City AM.

Some clubs could be required to hold more than £10m in liquid assets in order to satisfy conditions set by the Independent Football Regulator (IFR).

Those deemed higher risk will be asked to demonstrate cash reserves equivalent to five months of operating losses, which for some clubs would run into an eight-figure sum.

The proposal is part of the IFR’s consultation on reducing clubs’ risk to make them more resilient to sudden financial shocks such as losing owner funding. 

It comes after the IFR’s draft State of the Game report last month found that 94 per cent of professional clubs were loss-making, and a third were reliant on owner contributions to survive from month to month.

“The State of the Game report revealed just how serious the financial issues have become at some of our clubs. It has shown there is an urgent need to take action,” said IFR CEO Richard Monks. 

“Today we have set out how we plan to work with clubs to establish a more resilient financial base and to reduce their exposure. Our approach is proportionate to the financial risk and builds in a long lead time for clubs to enable them to stabilise their finances over the next three years.”

What it means for Premier League clubs

Clubs would have three years in which to build their cash reserves in order to meet the conditions by 2030. The requirements are likely to be less strict in the Premier League, where clubs are generally on a firmer financial footing, but they will be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

In the four divisions below the top flight, all clubs would be asked to hold liquid assets equivalent to their monthly wage bill as a minimum. Those designated as medium risk based on a number of factors would also have to hold cash reserves to cover two months of operating losses, with high risk clubs needing five months’ worth.

At the extreme end, teams with the biggest operating losses, minus amortisation, could be asked to hold £10m or more including the one month’s wages.

The IFR’s initial risk assessment will take place in 2027 and could be adjusted as teams’ fortunes improve or worsen over the following three years. It is hoped that clubs’ losses will come down in the intervening years, when EFL teams are likely to benefit from an improved financial redistribution agreement with the Premier League.

Two thirds of clubs’ liquid assets must be in cash, Gilts and US Treasuries, or money market funds. Up to a third can be in transfer receivables – staggered payments due from other clubs relating to player sales. Those who failed to meet liquidity requirements would face having stricter conditions imposed on their licence.

Shirtmaker TM Lewin is pivoting towards t-shirts and knitted sweaters as the AI-driven cutback in graduate hiring means fewer young workers need shirts and ties.

The retailer, which was established in 1898, has expanded its range of casualwear since returning to British high streets after its collapse into administration at the start of the decade. 

Dan Ferris, TM Lewin’s managing director, told City AM that its expansion away from solely producing formalwear has in part been driven by artificial intelligence, which he said has “diminished” the pool of young graduates taking up jobs in the City. 

The shirtmaker, which operated more than 150 shops during its peak in the mid-2010s, called in administrators in June 2020 after the Covid-19 pandemic saw demand for suits and ties plummet as lockdowns kept workers at home.

TM Lewin was bought out of administration in that year by Torque Brands, an arm of US-based private equity firm Stonebridge, before collapsing again in March 2022, as its new online-only model failed to bear fruit. 

The retailer has slowly begun opening new stores in recent months, at Square Mile sites including Bow Lane and Liverpool Street, but Ferris said it has been forced to expand its range of casual items like knitwear and shorts to keep up with changing demand.

He added the return to in-office work following the pandemic has boosted demand for suits and ties, though the retailer has been forced to adapt to new working habits.

“Most companies are at least one day working from home, so that’s one less day that you’re wearing a shirt,” he said. “If someone’s only in the office for three days, or if they’re wearing a polo or a knit when they are in the office, then that’s another day that you lose them. 

“I think a lot of office workers were wearing a suit and shirt five days a week pre-Covid, so it’s demonstrably, materially changed, and I don’t think, at least for the foreseeable future, it’s never going to go back to that.”

‘Graduate pool diminishing’

While TM Lewin used exclusively to sell formalwear, its range is now split half and half between suits and casualwear, Ferris said, with its recent best-sellers including rugby shirts and fisherman-style knitwear.

Asked whether TM Lewin is seeing lower formalwear demand from graduates, as City firms hand entry-level tasks to artificial intelligence agents, Ferris said: “Exactly. It reduces that pool of new customer acquisitions.

“We know that that pool is diminishing. Maybe it will grow again when everyone realises that you need people to do things as well as they are. But we’ve had to look to other areas to grow [while] that new graduate pool has diminished.”

The graduate hiring slowdown “is not just in finance,” he added. “You look at the tech industry, for example, and the layoffs are in the thousands almost every week? It’s obvious that AI is having an impact on employment.”

The number of graduate job vacancies in the UK fell to a record low in September, according to jobs platform Adzuna, with professional services giants like PwC and KPMG among those swinging the axe.

TM Lewin’s sales are 40 per cent higher year-on-year and it is set to open two new stores in November – in Victoria and Bluewater, Kent – but Ferris said the retailer will “never go back” to the sprawling footprint it had before its collapse. 

The shirtselling boss said high rents and rising business rates bills mean the company has had to “work really hard” to find viable locations for new stores. 

Ferris added he was “stunned by how little support” John Healey offered to retailers at last month’s Budget. The Chancellor was criticised for claiming to freeze business rates for high street businesses despite allowing the tax to continue rising with inflation.

“They’ve tried to do things, but the reality is, it’s just not helping retailers,” Ferris said. “You’ve got retailers going into administration consistently over the past two, three years, and this is not going to stop unless the government provides more support.”

Investors are ditching tech stocks for ones they believe can shield them from a market downturn as fears over the end of the AI bull market continue to grow.

So-called defensive sectors, which include consumer foosa, healthcare and utilities, have come back into favour in recent weeks as investors hunt for reliability amid wider global uncertainty.

“Investors grew increasingly sceptical of technology sector valuations and questioned the long-term funding plans for the massive AI build-out,” Schroders analysts said in a note to investors.

“Amid the major repricing of technology and the countries with tech-heavy equity markets, defensive sectors like energy, consumer staples and healthcare showed notable strength globally.”

Europe feels the benefit

While the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index has failed to reap the benefits of investors looking for safety, European stock markets boasting a range of consumer staples and healthcare stocks have recorded a sharp rise.

The Swiss Market Index rose a staggering 8.4 per cent, boosted by pharmaceutical firms Roche and Novartis.

Individual consumer staple companies who have seen their share price struggle against rising shipping and energy costs caused by the conflict in the Middle East also returned to gains.

Unilever, which owns brands such as Dove and Vaseline, has posted a 4.1 per cent rise in the last month, while Dettol owner Reckitt Benckiser and Diageo are up 8.1 per cent and 13 per cent respectively.

Downgrades and market jitters

Citi analysts dubbed the rotation “violent”, but noted that the outperformance could continue into the more cyclical part of the market next year.

“Earning revisions have decelerated and AI sentiment has plunged,” wrote Beata Manthey, head of European equity strategy at Citi in a note to clients where the bank explained its decision to downgrade a host of US and global tech stocks.

In 1997, my birth country fell apart. Albanian families had poured their savings into pyramid schemes that promised easy returns. When the schemes collapsed, the state collapsed with them – law and order almost vanished overnight. I have memories of sleeping next to an AK-47.

Unlike Khan, I am on the side of enterprise and those who generate wealth in our city. It is conducive to opportunity, which Labour is fast erasing as part of its crusade against business. Housebuilders are a prime example here –  if we are going to get homes built and the housebuilder makes profits, then it’s a win-win; more housing stock and a company willing to go and repeat it on another site. 

I’m not embarrassed by wealth creation. London’s next mayor shouldn’t be either. When it comes to our financial sector, we need a champion of the London Stock Exchange, not an ideologue who gets squeamish every time a private entity makes a bit of cash. So many opportunities squandered and London dreams never to be fulfilled. Our city cannot go on like this. 

We risk failing our banks too. Our tax burden on banks is estimated as 46.2 per cent by PwC, compared with 39 per cent in Frankfurt and just 28 per cent in New York. London gave me a chance, and I want every Londoner who works hard to feel that their ambition will be rewarded here, not exported elsewhere. That is London’s social contract, and that is the London dream. As Mayor, I will renew both. 

Sara Gezdari is prospective Conservative candidate for Mayor of London

In Britain, revenue jumped 10.2 per cent to €4.9bn, boosted by the Three merger, with Vodafone already delivering €50m in integration savings.

Duncan Ferris, analyst at Freetrade, said: “In the UK, headline numbers got a healthy injection from the Three merger, but underlying performance showed continued progress.”

Della Valle backs Talktalk rescue

Della Valle also backed the government’s intervention in the rescue of struggling broadband provider Talktalk, saying ministers had been right to act to protect customers.

“There was a matter of urgency given the circumstances, and so the government had to intervene on behalf of the customers, particularly considering the vulnerable customers in the Talktalk base,” she said.

However, she warned that the deal’s longer-term implications for competition would need careful consideration, particularly across the retail and wholesale broadband markets.

Asked whether Vodafone had raised concerns with the Competition and Markets Authority, Della Valle declined to comment on the ongoing process.
