]]> SRTD Biotech, a Jülich-based BioTech startup focused on developing next-generation precision mRNA therapeutics, has completed an oversubscribed €31.5 million Seed financing round.

The funding was led by Mérieux Equity Partners, with NRW.BANK and Boehringer Ingelheim Venture Fund joining the syndicate as co-leads. Lilly Ventures, HTGF, and the Freiburg-based family Office Anobis Asset also participated in the Seed round.

“We believe SRTD Biotech has the potential to redefine what is possible with mRNA therapeutics. Its highly differentiated technology addresses one of the key challenges facing the field today: achieving precise, selective therapeutic activity while limiting effects on healthy cells. 

“Having worked closely with the company to strengthen its strategy, build its leadership team and establish a scalable platform, we are delighted to lead this financing with our Mérieux Innovation 2 fund (MI2) alongside an exceptional group of investors,” said Kristin Thompson, Director at Mérieux Equity Partners. 

Founded in 2019 in Jülich by Dr. Bernd Hoffmann and Dr Heribert Bohlen, SRTD has developed an approach to cell-specific messenger RNA (mRNA) expression using intracellular RNA disease markers that activate the mRNA expression exclusively within target cells.

The company notes that these selectively expressed RNA (seRNA) constructs enable the controlled expression of therapeutic payloads within diseased cells, while minimising exposure in healthy tissue.

With this novel approach, SRTD plans to create safer, more effective, and differentiated RNA therapies that overcome limitations of non-selective mRNA expression and the constraints of targeting cell-surface proteins. 

SRTD is an integrated RNA therapeutics company combining three technology platforms: proprietary seRNA technology; a novel fusogenic LNP delivery platform to access the liver, lung, brain, and other organs; and a synthetic biology platform with bioinformatics and AI-driven RNA design capabilities. This integrated technology platform provides an end-to-end solution for generating differentiated RNA therapies across a wide range of therapeutic areas and indications.

After the financing round, Matthias Alder was appointed SRTD’s Chief Executive Officer. He has held senior C-suite roles (including CEO, COO and CBO) at publicly traded BioTech companies in the US and Europe. 

“The proceeds will enable SRTD to advance Bernd’s vision of delivering safe, effective, and differentiated RNA therapeutics to patients whose diseases remain inadequately addressed by current therapies,” said Alder.

Along with Matthias Alder, Dr. Heinz Koeppl has joined SRTD’s leadership team as the company’s Chief Technology Officer and the founder of SRTD’s synthetic biology platform. He is also a professor at the Technische Universität Darmstadt and the director of its Centre for Synthetic Biology. 

Together with Dr. Hoffmann, Dr. Koeppl will lead the scientific strategy of SRTD, with a particular focus on RNA marker identification and AI-based construct optimisation to ensure the selective and efficient activation of seRNA constructs.

Most recently, Dr. Jens Hennecke joined the executive leadership team of SRTD as its Chief Business Officer. He is responsible for driving business development and strategy, seeking to leverage the company’s platform through R&D collaborations in therapeutic areas and indications beyond SRTD’s own product pipeline.

“SRTD Biotech shows how cutting-edge research from North Rhine-Westphalia can open up new ways to treat many diseases with significant unmet medical needs. Bringing innovations like these from research into medical practice takes capital. With our investment in SRTD Biotech, we are helping a highly innovative company develop a promising new technology in NRW and scale it internationally from here,” Johanna Antonie Tjaden-Schulte, Member of NRW.BANK’s Managing Board. 

NRW.BANK is participating in SRTD Biotech’s financing round through its NRW.Venture EU Tech&Scale fund. Under its InvestEU partnership, a guarantee agreement with the European Commission enables the Düsseldorf-based bank to invest a total of up to €200 million in additional funding in young scale-ups through the fund.

The post OPINION: Building open source gives startups a head start, not a moat appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Every startup faces the same squeeze: big ambitions, small team and limited budget. Free open-source software, which can be used, modified, and redistributed under its license, can help founders ease the squeeze. It lets a small startup build products that once required a large engineering department.

But a shortcut is not a strategy. To make good use of open source, founders must decide what they should build themselves, what to borrow, and which skills their team needs to retain. Here is what to consider, from saving time and standing out to staying secure and talking to investors.

Saving time

Microsoft’s Edge browser shows how this can work. I co-authored a study of its move to Chromium, the open-source engine also behind Google’s Chrome, found faster releases and closer alignment with Chrome’s supported web features. Edge remained Microsoft’s own product, on a shared foundation. For founders, the question is how much development work a shared foundation can save, and what trade-offs come with it.

Artificial intelligence offers a similar shortcut. Free toolkits such as TensorFlow and PyTorch help developers build AI applications. “Open-weight” models, such as Meta’s Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen, let teams download an AI system that has already been trained and adapt it, rather than start from scratch.

But open-weight does not necessarily mean open source. Founders should read the license carefully: downloading a model does not necessarily provide access to its training data or unrestricted rights to sell products built on it.

Before committing, startups should build a small prototype around a real customer task. A polished demo can hide missing features, thin documentation or fiddly integration work. Founders should also factor in the costs of computing power and upkeep. Access to the code lets teams tailor software or run it in a customer’s own systems, provided they have the skills and resources to manage it.

Standing out

If competitors can use the same technology, a startup needs to give customers a reason to choose its product. That might mean specialist features, smoother links with the systems customers already use, or reliable support. Founders can use the development time saved to find out what customers value enough to pay for.

Take an AI tool for manufacturers. It could pair a widely available model with a factory’s equipment records and tests designed around how engineers work. Tying the technology to a real job can make a product useful even when the model underneath is available to everyone.

Some companies make money from their own open code. Strapi, a French startup, offers a free content management system and charges for extra features and support. Founders who publish their code need to be equally clear about what customers pay for. They also need to allow time for users’ questions, documentation and outside contributions.

Keeping expertise in-house

Startups need staff who understand how the product works and can change it. In research I led on German firms, I found that product innovation was strongest among companies that outsourced a moderate amount of IT work. In related research I co-authored, we found that excessive reliance on outsourcing raises the risk of intellectual-property infringement.

The practical question for founders is which skills they need to retain as they draw on outside work. Early choices can become expensive to reverse. A team learns one framework; data takes on its format, and other parts of the product grow around it.

Before the business relies on a critical component, the team should test how easily it could be replaced. Design decisions and the ability to investigate failures should stay within the team. When working with outside developers, founders should agree who owns the work and what stays confidential.

Engineers also need time to experiment. If all their effort goes into stitching together other people’s software, they may struggle to build the know-how needed for the startup’s next product.

Maintenance and security

Joining an open-source community can help a startup’s developers learn. Research on larger companies found that contributors got more value from using open source, partly through feedback from other developers.

An active community can help spot and fix problems, but security still needs an owner inside the startup. 

The Open-Source Security Foundation advises tracking outside components, checking their origins and maintenance, and monitoring newly discovered vulnerabilities. Someone within the startup should be responsible for testing and installing updates.

Some popular projects rely on a single volunteer. Paid support may be worthwhile for critical components, while startups publishing their own code also need time for handling security reports and maintaining new versions.

Making the case to investors

Founders should show what the head start delivered, whether they have a working product, paying customers, or evidence of demand. They should explain what they didn’t have to build because they used open source, and what they developed themselves.

Our study found that US startups that engaged with outside projects on GitHub, a popular code-sharing site, were more likely to have raised their first funding round. The link was stronger for novel technologies and weaker in crowded markets. However, the research does not imply that publishing open source code alone will win over investors.

Founders should be ready to explain their own contribution to the product, the cost of maintaining it and how they would manage problems with a critical dependency. The test is whether open source helps them build something customers value while leaving the team able to maintain and improve it.

]]> Onodrim, the Dutch European defence and industrial scale-up platform, has closed a €268.01 million ($300 million) Series A funding round at a €1.16 billion ($1.3 billion) valuation.

The funding round was led by US investment group Lux Capital, with participation from existing investors General Catalyst and Lakestar, alongside Altimeter, Strike Capital, 137 Ventures, and 8090, Expeditions, among others. The company had raised a €40.20 million ($45 million) Seed round earlier this year, backed by General Catalyst, Lakestar, and Founders Fund, the VC arm of tech billionaire and Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel.

“Europe needs a stronger industrial foundation to meet the security challenges ahead. We see an enormous opportunity to bring a new model of ownership and investment to the continent’s most important businesses,” said Brandon Reeves, Partner at Lux Capital.

Founded in 2026 by Aistis Šimaitis, Alexander Blessing, and Christian Garrett, Onodrim, like Palantir, takes its name from The Lord of the Rings: the Elvish term for the tree-like Ents, creatures roused to go to war. The name reflects the company’s stated mission of waking up the sleeping giants of European manufacturing.

Šimaitis, co-founder and CEO, is a former adviser to the Lithuanian government and one of Palantir’s first hires in Europe in 2013. Blessing, co-founder and CTO, previously served as a Forward Deployed Engineer at Palantir and was closely involved in developing and deploying Palantir’s flagship Foundry software platform, used by companies and governments to streamline data and digitise workflows. Garrett, Partner at 137 Ventures, is also a co-founder.

Onodrim acquires controlling stakes in established European defence, aerospace, and industrial businesses, particularly small and medium-sized, founder-led family companies. It then scales them up using permanent capital, technology, and business development expertise. The company also encourages existing founders to remain and help grow their businesses as part of the Onodrim group. It expects to announce its first acquisitions in the coming months.

“Europe has no shortage of exceptional companies. The challenge has been access to the resources needed to help them grow at the scale and speed the moment demands. We are bringing permanent capital, technology and world-class operators to Europe’s best companies, giving them the resources to expand, compete and strengthen the continent’s defence industrial base,” said Šimaitis, co-founder and CEO of Onodrim.

European defence companies are sitting on record order backlogs following the continent’s sharp increase in military spending after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine over four years ago. Most of these companies are struggling to expand capacity fast enough to meet government orders. Onodrim says the market is not only under significant pressure but it is also an opportunity for an operator to plug the gap and build Europe’s defence sovereignty.

“Our approach at Onodrim is rooted in long-term partnership and collaboration. We believe Europe’s industrial champions are built by investing in great businesses, empowering the people behind them and giving them the resources to grow for the long term,” said Blessing, co-founder and CTO, Onodrim

The fresh capital will fund Onodrim’s acquisition programme. It is also expanding its European presence by opening Onodrim Germany in Munich and Onodrim Italy in Turin, joining its existing offices in Amsterdam, London and Vilnius. The company says it has already identified several targets but declined to name them. Additionally, Onodrim has flagged supply chain bottlenecks in areas including propulsion systems for drones, sensing and radar, energetics used in explosives, and aero-structures as priority areas.

]]> BlackPeak Capital, a Bulgarian private equity firm, today announced the first close of BlackPeak Southeast Europe Growth Equity Fund II SCSp (BPSEEF II) at €125 million to invest in fast-growing companies across Southeast Europe, with Bulgaria, Romania, Croatia, Slovenia and Serbia as its primary markets

BPSEEF II is backed by returning anchor investors from BPSEEF I, including the European Investment Fund (EIF), the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), Erste Asset Management and the International Finance Corporation (IFC). The EIF has committed €35 million comprising €10 million under the Romania Recovery Equity Fund and €25 million under the Bulgaria Recovery and Resilience Plan. The EBRD and IFC have committed €30 million and €20 million respectively.

The Fund also welcomes HBOR, the Croatian Bank for Reconstruction and Development, and Universal Pension Fund Doverie, Bulgaria’s largest pension fund, together with regional private investors.

Ivailo Gospodinov, Managing Partner at BlackPeak Capital, says: “Five years ago we spent much of our time explaining the investment case for Southeast Europe. Today, the region remains one of the fastest growing in Europe and its success stories increasingly make that case on their own. We see a new generation of ambitious founders who have built leaders in their specific niches. What these companies lack is growth capital at the scale they need and expertise to expand internationally. BPSEEF II is specifically designed to address that gap.”

BlackPeak’s new fund follows other European investment fund closes in 2026, including fellow Sofia-based LAUNCHub Ventures’ €65 million first close to support early-stage startups across Central and Southeast Europe, and Warsaw-based Montis VC’s €50 million first close targeting energy and industrial technology.

Elsewhere, Paris-based SlateVC raised €132 million, while UK-based Molten Ventures secured €203 million for its growth fund. Together with BlackPeak’s €125 million, these closes represent €575 million.

EU-Startups previously covered BlackPeak’s €7 million investment in Croatia’s Fasal Bio, illustrating its existing investment activity in the region.

Rossen Ivanov, Managing Partner at BlackPeak Capital, adds: “With BPSEEF I, we scaled our team regionally and demonstrated that our strategy of investing in minority growth deals with a strong buy-and-build focus, both regionally and globally, delivers excellent results. With BPSEEF II, we benefit from an already strong pipeline and deep insight into sectors where we believe structural growth is ahead.”

Established in 2014, BlackPeak Capital has raised over €280 million in cumulative commitments across three funds and has on-the-ground presence in Sofia, Bucharest, Zagreb, Belgrade, Ljubljana and Vienna.

At first close, BPSEEF II has nearly matched its predecessor’s €126 million final size. BPSEEF I started in 2021 and had a final size of €126 million. BPSEEF I invested in 11 companies and completed 16 add-on acquisitions, delivering revenue growth of 34% annually over the last five years. The predecessor fund has reportedly already returned a significant part of the invested capital following the successful exit from euShipments.com to Austrian Post and two further partial exits from GenePlanet and Wiser Technology.

The new Fund is targeting €150 million, with a hard cap of €200 million, and expects to hold its final close in 2027.

BPSEEF II will invest €7 – 20 million per transaction. The Fund may also invest opportunistically across the wider Central and Eastern European region, including Poland, Hungary, Slovakia, the Baltic states and other Western Balkan markets.

The Fund will take significant minority or majority stakes, partnering with founders and providing the capital, network and expertise to scale their businesses into regional and global leaders. Generalist by design, BPSEEF II will focus on broad investment themes including e-commerce, healthcare, digitalisation, sustainability, and others.

The Fund expects to build a portfolio of 10 to 12 companies.

Niklas Pichler, Managing Partner at BlackPeak Capital, says: “Our goal is to help ambitious regional businesses become international leaders. We combine growth capital with practical support in entering new markets, making acquisitions and strengthening management teams. As an active partner, we work closely with founders, supporting their vision while helping them build the capabilities needed for the next stage of growth.”

BlackPeak expects to make its first investments from BPSEEF II at the beginning of 2027.

]]> Calogena, a French nuclear startup developing a small modular reactor (SMR) designed to supply low-carbon heat to district heating networks, has secured €40 million.

The funding came in the form of a grant from the European Commission’s Innovation Fund ,and it marks the first time that European funding has been given to an SMR earmarked for the direct construction of a commercial facility.

“This funding marks a major milestone for Calogena. Having developed our technology and brought it to industrial scale, we are now entering the construction phase of our first commercial reactor,” said Julien Dereux, Executive Chairman of Calogena.

Calogena was founded in 2021 as a subsidiary of Groupe Gorgé, a Paris-based high-tech industrial group with approximately 3,500 employees and €600 million in revenue. The company is developing a 30-thermal-megawatt, water-cooled SMR specifically designed to decarbonise district heating networks.

Its reactor is based on pool-type research reactor technology, a design proven in hundreds of installations worldwide. It operates at low temperature (100°C) and low pressure (6 bar), less than a bicycle tyre, making it simpler and safer to operate than conventional power reactors.

Another strength of Calogena’s SMR is its compact footprint, requiring just 3,000 square metres of land and under 1,000 square metres of building. The design also does not require major water or electricity supply, and refuelling requires only one lorry delivery every two years. Each module can supply heat to around 20,000 households and produces less than 80ml of nuclear water over a lifetime of use.

The grant follows more than €50 million already secured under France’s national industrial strategy programme, France 2030, which helped the company develop its technology and bring it to industrial readiness. 

The €40 million grant will be used to fund the construction of Calogena’s first commercial reactor in Pierrelatte, which would serve as the company’s inaugural commercial reference project. The company says the town will receive locally produced, low-carbon heat, an alternative to the carbon-intensive and largely imported energy sources that currently account for nearly one-third of Europe’s total energy demand. 

“The European Commission’s support confirms the maturity of our project and its potential to address one of Europe’s major energy challenges: producing local, low-carbon, cost-competitive heat at scale while strengthening energy sovereignty. Pierrelatte would be our first commercial reference and should pave the way for wider deployment across Europe,” added Dereux.

In addition to the Pierrelatte project, the company is also pursuing projects across Europe and is in contention to supply more than fifteen reactors in Finland, where it opened a subsidiary in 2025. In June, Calogena signed a cooperation agreement with Veolia, a European leader in district heating, to explore the deployment of its SMRs across Central and Eastern Europe.

As the European district heating market is projected to reach around 1,000 TWh by 2050, Calogena argues that its technology can provide a price-stable, long-term solution for energy sovereignty. It is targeting initial deployments from 2030, with its first commercial reactor in Pierrelatte scheduled to go live in 2032.

]]> Marble Imaging, a Bremen-based big data Earth Observation (EO) company setting up Germany’s first commercial constellation of very-high-resolution (VHR) satellites, has raised an additional €6 million in a Seed extension round led by Cherry Ventures. 

In December 2025, the company announced it had closed an oversubscribed €5.3 million Seed round led by High-Tech Gründerfonds, bringing total funding to €11.3 million.

“To make better decisions, data access must be immediate and actionable. Europe and many of its global partners lack this capability today. We at Marble are determined to close this gap, and Cherry’s trust helps us achieve this faster,” said Robert Hook, co-founder and CEO of Marble Imaging. 

Founded in August 2023 by Hook, Dr. Gopika Suresh, Alexander Epp, and Dr. Raul Scarlat, Marble Imaging is building its constellation of VHR satellites to provide up to hourly EO data and analytics for time-critical insights of the planet.

According to the company, the data and derived EO-based analytics will be vital in supporting rapid decision-making for defence, climate security, crisis and disaster management, green and sustainable energy transitions, infrastructure and mobility, and more.

It already offers advanced data analysis services, including object detection for situational intelligence, terrain analysis and trafficability assessment, coastal asset monitoring and land cover classification.

Marble highlighted that although VHR imagery is a core input for security and commercial intelligence, Europe and many of its partners rely on non-European providers. “This makes them vulnerable to being cut off from coverage over key areas of interest, as materialised in Ukraine or the Strait of Hormuz, creating massive economic as well as security knowledge gaps,” it stated. 

Marble is therefore setting up Germany’s first commercial constellation of very-high-resolution (VHR) satellites. The German startup is also building an AI-powered analytics platform that converts multi-source data into insights. It also notes that as Marble’s constellation scales, the interplay of these segments will create a uniquely well-trained AI solution that delivers actionable decision support for users in the defence, civil security, and critical infrastructure sectors, and beyond.

“Europe needs its own eyes in space, and Marble Imaging is building them. They are using AI to turn pixels into answers, exactly what government and defence customers need. This team has spent their careers in the industry and knows what it takes to build something very big. The product Marble will deliver doesn’t exist in Europe yet, but we’re convinced it has to,” said Filip Dames, Founding Partner at Cherry Ventures.

Marble’s first satellite, Marble Sat-1, is fully funded, has completed pre-flight testing and is scheduled to launch in early 2027. It is designed to capture imagery at up to 0.7 m spatial resolution in the visible and near-infrared spectrum and will also gather data in the shortwave infrared spectrum. 

The company plans to use this capital to accelerate the scaling of its constellation, with a goal of 30 satellites by 2030. It will accelerate satellite and launch procurement for Germany’s first commercial very high-resolution constellation

“Scaling from here is a question of capital, not technology. The demand is proven, the hardware comes from experienced suppliers, and our software is already used by paying customers. We need to invest in more satellite capability in space, and this round accelerates our path to delivering sovereign intelligence with a European identity – stable access, transparency and democratic governance that partners around the world can count on,” said Hook.

Hera, the European Space Agency’s first mission for planetary defence, arrives at its target body during November, with the goal of gathering precious data on the kinetic impact method of asteroid deflection – while also solving various scientific enigmas.

The small-car-sized spacecraft is headed to the 151-m-diameter Dimorphos asteroid, which orbits in turn around its 780-m Didymos parent. Dimorphos is already historic as the first object in the Solar System to have had its orbit changed by human action – when NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted it on 26 September 2022.

DART’s impact caused a brightening visible from distant Earth telescopes, but nobody knows what it did to Dimorphos itself. Hera is going there to perform a close-up crash site survey, to help turn DART’s kinetic impact experiment into a well understood planetary defence deflection technique.

Scientists are hoping for bonus science as well. Past spacecraft close encounters have revealed asteroids to be dynamic environments with complex histories – and many outstanding questions still to be answered. Here are 10 asteroid mysteries that Hera will explore.

US Air Force explores new defences https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/usaf-f35-netting-tyndall-drone-protection/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 17:13:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56267 The US Air Force is looking for contractors to install anti-drone netting to help protect F-35 Joint Strike Fighters amid growing concerns over drone threats.

The post Could netting protect F-35s from drones? US Air Force explores new defences appeared first on AGN.

]]> The US Air Force is looking to protect its F-35A fighter jets at Tyndall Air Force Base in Florida with netting, according to reports.

Netting remains one of the most affordable, quickest, and reliable layers of protection for parked aircraft from small UAS threats.

The Air Force’s 325th Contracting Squadron at Tyndall has issued a request for information entitled “Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (C-UAS) Netting Installation for Aircraft Sunshade Structures.”

It explained that the USAF is conducting market research for the installation of netting on existing aircraft sunshade structures. The contract is particularly focused on small businesses.

The Air Force stated, “The Government is also interested in unique and innovative solutions, including any proof-of-concept or operational C-UAS netting installations already fielded or under evaluation at other Department of Defense installations.”

Protecting USAF’s F-35A stealth fighters

While a number of defence-tech companies are currently working on developing an array of effective counter-UAS solutions, one of the most effective solutions remains an old-fashioned net or other physical barrier.

In the procurement notice, the requirements are for a contractor to install counter-UAV netting on all four sides of six existing aircraft sunshade structures. Each structure is around 630 feet long, 65 feet wide, and 30 feet high.

The War Zone identifies that these shelters are designed to accommodate up to six F-35A stealth fighters at a time. Tyndall is a major hub for the United States Air Force’s F-35 operations and is located in Florida’s Panhandle.

The topic of netting over US fighter jets is not new. Plans have been floated to erect netting around sunshade-type shelters for F-22 Raptors stationed at Langley after mysterious late 2023 drone incursions.

Across the United States and Europe, there have been numerous reports of unexplained drones flying over air force bases and airports.

Realistically, these small drones likely present the biggest aerial threat to Allied parked aircraft in their mainland home bases in peacetime.

Notably, in 2026, saboteurs attempted to destroy Ukrainian Antonov An-124 Ruslan transports parked at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport. At least one explosive-laden drone is reported to have found its mark but failed to explode.

Drones or birds? The detection challenge behind NATO’s false alarm Drones or birds? The detection challenge behind NATO’s false alarm

An effective solution against small FPV-type drones

Netting may be ineffective against heavier one-way attack drones, missiles, and certain types of warheads, but they are very effective against many types of lower-end FPV-type drones.

The Air Force explicitly identifies the purpose as blocking Group 1 “small” drones from striking the aircraft.

— Thomas van Linge (@ThomasVLinge) September 10, 2026

Netting may have been enough to block Ukrainian FPV strikes on Russian bombers during Operation Spider Web.

More recently, opposition fighters in Myanmar (Burma) struck junta Yak-130 light combat aircraft in their hangars at Mandalay for the first time with small drones. The outcome was unclear, but released footage appears to show the drones struggling to bypass the protective netting.

In Ukraine, roads and entire neighbourhoods near the frontline are now often encased in netting.

]]> China highlights GJ-11 combat drone ahead of air force anniversary https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/china-gj11-stealth-drone-new-footage/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 16:03:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56206 New images and state reporting reveals more of China's new higher-end stealth strike and loyal wingman drone that appears to be entering service.

The post China highlights GJ-11 combat drone ahead of air force anniversary appeared first on AGN.

]]> Chinese state media has released new images of its GJ-11 stealth combat drone, which publicly flew for the first time in a November 2025 PLAAF video. The GJ-11 is believed to have entered service.

The stealthy drone is a flying wing and is known in China as the Xuanlong, or Dark Dragon. It was first unveiled in China’s 2019 National Day military parade in Beijing

China’s CCTV unveils detailed pictures of its GJ-11 drone

The video of the drone appeared in a report by China’s CCTV state broadcaster in a countdown to tomorrow’s 77th anniversary of the PLA Air Force.

Images provide a good look at the drone, including its large internal weapon bay, which has been designed to carry relatively large missiles. The GJ-11 has a shielded jet nozzle, low-visibility coating, and a faceted optical window mounted beneath the nose.

According to reporting by the South China Morning Post, this appears similar to the electro-optical targeting system found on China’s leading J-20 fighter.

Like various US designs, including the upcoming Lockheed Martin Vectis, the GJ-11 has its air intake on top of its fuselage. It also bears a flattened tail section.

The state-run English-language outlet, Global Times, reported that CCTV also revealed: “Two post-95s drone operators Shi Xiaoran and Fu Ting, are among the first batch of female drone operators trained independently by the PLA Air Force.”

Role of the GJ-11 stealth combat drone

Chinese state TV characterized the GJ-11 as a pioneer and a pathfinder. Core future missions include ground strikes and serving as a loyal wingman drone for fighter jets.

A video shows it flying in formation with a J-20 stealth fighter and J-16D electronic warfare aircraft, although it is unclear if they are teaming.

China released a video a year ago showing it firing a live PL-15 air-to-air missile.

The CCTV report stated that the GJ-11, operating in coordination with another drone, “can serve as the eyes of crewed fighter jets, conducting forward reconnaissance to identify enemy air defence systems.”

It added, “They can also act as decoys to draw enemy fire and expose hostile positions, or even function as airborne weapons platforms, launching guided munitions under the direction of manned aircraft.”

Its internal weapons bay is capable of accommodating a variety of air-to-surface munitions. The design is reported to provide strong stealth and endurance, while also being able to carry out suppression of enemy air defence (SEAD) missions.

China’s B-2-sized stealth drones spotted at Malan test base in satellite imagery China’s B-2-sized stealth drones spotted at Malan test base in satellite imagery

The GJ-11’s development & naval variant

Cloud cover has been an issue for targeting. The state report featured operator Shi Xiaoran saying the GJ-11 almost failed to locate its target during its first live-fire test on account of thick cloud cover.

Circling back for another pass, the drone is reported to have targeted and hit the target. The CCTV did not elaborate on the circumstances.

China has shown for the first time how operators work the Gongji-11 (GJ-11) strike drone, which it describes as a “door-kicking tool” meant to break through enemy air defenses first. The drone is meant to destroy key targets and open the way for crewed aircraft. Operator Shi Xiaoran said a single combat sortie usually lasts more than six hours, and some operations can run for several days.

China’s new stealth drone is believed to have been developed and tested at the PLA AF base in Malan, Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region.

It also has a carrier-based naval variant, the GJ-21. That drone is reported to have successfully carried out a take-off and landing operation on the PLAN’s Type 076 Sichuan amphibious assault ship last week.

]]> Former bmibaby Boeing 737 lowered into Derbyshire garden as underground bunker takes shape https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/former-bmibaby-boeing-737-doomsday-bunker/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 15:01:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56248 The unusual structure will double up as an underground entertainment space when not being used as a doomsday bunker.

The post Former bmibaby Boeing 737 lowered into Derbyshire garden as underground bunker takes shape appeared first on AGN.

]]> A retired bmibaby Boeing 737-500 has taken a major step towards an unusual second life after being lowered into a large hole in a Derbyshire garden using a huge crane.

Dave Billings, a 45-year-old engineer, entrepreneur and YouTube creator from Hilton, Derbyshire, has successfully moved the aircraft fuselage into position as part of his ambitious plan to create an underground doomsday bunker beneath his property.

The operation, which took place on 20 October, involved a large crane, five volunteers and several crane operators. The remarkable lifting operation marks a significant milestone in a project that was first reported by Aerospace Global News in February this year and attracted attention earlier this year when Billings revealed he had purchased the aircraft section for just £4,000.

Now that the former passenger cabin is in the ground, work is progressing on transforming it into an underground ‘man cave’, which will eventually connect to an existing underground room beneath his garden.

Boeing 737 lowered into garden using huge crane

Getting a retired passenger aircraft into a back garden was never going to be a straightforward undertaking. As reported by the BBC, after purchasing the fuselage through Facebook Marketplace, Billings faced the challenge of transporting the enormous structure to his home and finding a way to install it underground.

The solution involved digging a substantial hole, preparing special foundations and bringing in a large crane to lower the aircraft into position. Five volunteers helped with the operation, while the crane operators carefully manoeuvred the fuselage into its new home.

Billings documented the process from several different angles for his YouTube channel (‘Tornado Dave’), including footage captured using an action camera mounted on the crane jib itself.

He has also used 3D printing to produce a scale model showing how the aircraft section will connect to the existing underground accommodation.

Speaking about the aircraft’s dimensions, Billingsted told the BBC that the aircraft’s size was even more impressive in reality than it had appeared in photographs.

However, he believes the width makes it particularly suitable for conversion into a usable entertainment space (when not being used as a doomsday bunker).

From Facebook Marketplace purchase to underground bunker

The unusual project began when Billings spotted the Boeing 737 fuselage advertised on Facebook Marketplace. Having immediately recognised its potential, he decided to make an offer of £4,000.

Initially, not everyone shared his enthusiasm. One friend thought the idea was silly, while his wife Beth questioned why he wanted to purchase what she considered a pile of junk.

However, his seven-year-old son was considerably more supportive, encouraging his father to go ahead with the purchase.

Billings has since adapted the aircraft section to create an underground recreational space, which will ultimately become part of a larger network of underground rooms and tunnels at his property.

He has considered installing games machines, although the available space will not accommodate a full-sized pool table. He hopes to have the project completed by February 2027 and intends to apply for retrospective planning permission from the local authority.

The former bmibaby Boeing has an interesting history

The aircraft being transformed is a Boeing 737-500, originally registered as G-BVKB. Built in 1993, the aircraft spent much of its operational life flying passengers on domestic and European routes.

It initially served with British Midland Airways before transferring to its low-cost subsidiary bmibaby in 2002.

During its time with bmibaby, the aircraft was reconfigured to accommodate 131 passengers in an all-economy layout. It operated from the airline’s bases at East Midlands, Manchester and Cardiff, carrying holidaymakers to popular destinations including Alicante, Malaga and Faro.

In 2009, the aircraft even received a special name, Pudsey Baby, to support that year’s BBC Children in Need appeal.

After bmibaby closed in 2012, the aircraft was retired, stored at Norwich Airport, and later transported to Bruntingthorpe in Leicestershire in 2013 for dismantling and parts recovery.

Its fuselage was divided into sections, with the forward portion eventually converted into a camper trailer. Billings acquired part of the rear fuselage, retaining some recognisable passenger-aircraft features.

Tornado Dave documenting the aircraft’s unusual transformation

Billings has been sharing his engineering and construction projects on YouTube since 2021 through his channel, Tornado Dave, which now has more than 326,000 subscribers.

His interest in creating unusual engineering projects developed following his involvement with Guy’s Garage, the television programme featuring presenter and former motorcycle racer Guy Martin.

The Boeing 737 conversion has become one of his most unusual projects, attracting attention from aviation enthusiasts and viewers interested in engineering and unconventional construction.

The channel has also allowed Billings to document the practical challenges of moving, positioning and converting such a large aircraft structure.

What happens next for the underground Boeing 737 bunker?

With the fuselage now safely lowered into its prepared foundations, attention turns to completing the underground structure and connecting it to the existing accommodation beneath the garden.

The finished space is intended to be a recreational retreat rather than a conventional aviation attraction, although its unusual origins are certain to make it a talking point.

For a Boeing 737 that once carried thousands of passengers across the UK and Europe, its new role is certainly unexpected. After being bought for £4,000, the former bmibaby aircraft is now well on its way to becoming one of Britain’s most unusual garden conversions.

]]> NASA is moving ahead with its plans to send a nuclear-powered rover to the Moon’s South Pole in 2028, alongside new transportation contracts worth approximately $1.3 billion and the selection of eight companies to compete for future lunar cargo deliveries.

The six-wheeled rover, named Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration or PROMISE, will search for water ice and other resources that could support a permanent human presence on the Moon.

Built largely from existing hardware developed for NASA’s Curiosity and Perseverance Mars missions, it will be able to operate through long lunar nights and inside permanently shadowed craters where solar-powered vehicles face significant limitations.

The announcements, made at the MAX POWER aerospace expo at Kennedy Space Center in Florida on 7 November, mark another step in NASA’s effort to establish a lunar outpost before moving towards sustained human operations. The agency is developing a network of commercial landers, orbital transportation vehicles, communications systems and surface infrastructure intended to support astronauts returning to the Moon.

“We are building the Moon Base mission by mission,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said. “When our astronauts return to the Moon, they will arrive with the first elements of the Moon Base already waiting for them on the surface.”

Eight companies compete for lunar deliveries

NASA has selected Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines, ispace-US, Lockheed Martin Space, Northrop Grumman Space Systems, SpaceX and Voyager Technologies for the next phase of its Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) programme.

The companies will be eligible to compete for contracts to deliver scientific instruments, technology and infrastructure to the lunar surface. Selection does not guarantee individual missions.

The new CLPS 2 framework has a combined maximum value of $10 billion over 10 years. NASA has also raised the ceiling of the existing CLPS contract from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion to support the initial phase of Moon Base development.

The original contract remains in place until November 2028, with deliveries under awarded missions permitted through November 2033.

NASA is expanding its transportation arrangements because a lunar settlement will require regular deliveries of equipment, supplies and scientific payloads. Some cargo will need to be transferred between orbits before landers carry it to the surface.

Nuclear-powered rover built from Mars hardware

Among the new developments is PROMISE, designed to explore the lunar South Pole and investigate resources that could support astronauts living there.

The PROMISE will be built at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California using spare flight components and engineering test hardware developed for the Curiosity and Perseverance Mars missions.

Engineers will repurpose the electronics, structure and mobility system of Curiosity’s engineering test vehicle, combining them with other existing rover components. NASA says this approach will reduce development costs and shorten testing.

PROMISE will use a multi-mission radioisotope thermoelectric generator, which converts heat from radioactive decay into electricity. Unlike a solar-powered rover, it will be able to operate during the long lunar night and explore permanently shadowed craters where sunlight does not reach the surface.

Those regions are particularly important because scientists believe some contain water ice and other frozen materials. Determining where these resources occur, and how accessible they are, will influence decisions about future landing sites and infrastructure.

The SUV-sized rover will carry a drill capable of reaching approximately one metre below the surface, alongside instruments to examine the chemical composition of lunar soil, detect volatile materials and measure radiation and temperature.

Its equipment will also include NASA’s High Performance Spaceflight Computing system and technology for more autonomous operations.

NASA is targeting a launch in late 2028 and an 18-month primary mission.

Blue Origin has received a $94 million base contract, with a further $140 million option dependent on performance, to deliver PROMISE using its Blue Moon Mark 1 lander. The award expands an earlier task order issued in May 2026 for the delivery of two lunar terrain vehicles.

Building a transport network between Earth and Moon

The six new transportation task orders were awarded to Arrow Science and Technology, Blue Origin and Impulse Space under NASA’s Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare programme.

They cover launch integration and transportation services for missions designed to test communications, navigation and cargo movement between Earth orbit and the Moon.

One mission will carry CAPSTONE 02 into deep space to demonstrate navigation, communications and proximity operations around the Moon.

Another group of missions will deploy MoonFall, a fleet of highly mobile robotic drones intended to investigate terrain near the lunar South Pole. These vehicles are designed to reach locations that conventional rovers may find difficult to access.

Other missions will test commercial orbital transfer vehicles capable of moving cargo through different orbits. NASA wants to establish whether these spacecraft can help position landers and payloads more efficiently for lunar deliveries.

Launch vehicles expected to support the work include Blue Origin’s New Glenn, Relativity Space’s Terran R and SpaceX’s Falcon 9. In-space transportation will involve spacecraft supplied by Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Impulse Space and Quantum Space.
The six task orders fall under the broader VADR contract, which has a $5 billion maximum value.

SpaceX Starship to deploy lunar communications satellites

NASA has separately selected SpaceX to launch communications satellites into cislunar space aboard Starship in 2028.

The mission, awarded under an existing lunar logistics contract, will demonstrate capabilities needed for a communications network linking astronauts, spacecraft, ground controllers and future lunar installations.

On the Moon itself, NASA is developing a smaller demonstration system called the Mini-Communications and Solar Tower, or miniCAST.

Honeybee Robotics will supply energy storage technology, Redwire will provide power generation components and Yank Technologies will contribute wireless power transfer hardware.

NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama will assemble and test the equipment before its planned delivery to the lunar surface. The initial effort involves individual components rather than a complete operational power network.

A separate solicitation for integrated lunar power systems is expected in early 2027.

Carlos Garcia-Galan, manager of NASA’s Moon Base Programme, said the agency had consolidated several activities into a more coordinated approach to lunar development.

“Most importantly, we’ve taken action, awarding new contracts and forging new partnerships to accelerate development,” he said.

NASA also plans to seek additional scientific and engineering data through its NextSTEP-3 B initiative to help resolve outstanding questions about operating a permanent base.

The immediate task is to demonstrate that robotic exploration, commercial transportation, communications and power systems can work together before astronauts begin extended operations on the lunar surface.

]]> Larnaca-based Cyprus Airways has been expanding rapidly over the last few years. Most recently, it announced plans to launch a daily service to London Stansted Airport beginning in April 2027.

It will join Athens as one of the airline’s most competitive routes with five other carriers flying to the Mediterranean city from various London gateways.

Aside from some charter operations that help cushion lower demand, it hopes its route expansion helps drive interest in Cyprus. He points to Athens as a good example, which has been able to partially smooth out demand peaks and troughs as interest in travel expands beyond the summer months.

It will continue to increase its share of transit passengers, leveraging both online connections into its own network via Larnaca, but also through partner airlines. Pascalis describes this as “imperative” to ease seasonal demand fluctuations.

Pascalis says less than 1% of its passengers currently transit. “We’re trying to increase it two-, three- or fourfold, to get to something that gives us some real connectivity between our different destinations.”

Cyprus Airways also hopes to build on its cooperation with Air France to funnel additional passengers to/from North America for instance, as well as its partnership with flydubai.

Cyprus Airways has been faced with several operational and commercial challenges over the last few years. When asked if Cyprus Airways was interested, the CEO said: “We have not yet taken a decision on where we’re going to go for any additional lift we’re looking at for 2028, so anything is open. We could go for additional A320s or A220s.”

He pointed to the current fuel crisis as a constraint to its future growth. “So in order to take decisions on further expansion, we also need to see the fuel price subsiding, and some stability in the geopolitics of the region.”

]]> Boeing plans to cut about 5% of its Commercial Aeroplanes workforce after slowing plans to raise jet production. The division will reduce staffing through attrition and involuntary redundancies, with layoff notices expected to begin as early as December.

Stephanie Pope, president and chief executive of Boeing Commercial Aeroplanes, told employees on 9 November that the company was giving its factories and suppliers more time to stabilise production. The revised output plans leave the division with more staff than it needs.

Boeing expects layoff notices to begin in December

Boeing’s published employment figures show the division’s headcount stood at 50,494 at the end of December 2025. 

“Adjusting our production schedules and reducing aircraft output puts us in an overstaffed position,” Pope wrote in the internal memo, as reported by FOX 13 Seattle, which obtained the email from Boeing communications officials. 

Boeing will begin notifying affected employees in December. A 5% reduction in the workforce could mean layoffs for over 2,500 employees around the holidays. 

“I know how difficult these actions are and the impact they will have on all of us, our families, and our communities. We will never take that lightly,” Pope said.

The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers’ District 751 told Axios it had been notified of the company’s plans. The union said it did not yet know which employees would be affected or how many.

Boeing targets 52 737s a month in late 2027

Boeing began moving from 42 to 47 737s a month in the second quarter, with approval from the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). In July, chief executive Kelly Ortberg said he expected factory rollouts to reach 47 a month that summer.

However, on Boeing’s 27 October earnings call, Ortberg said it would take until 2027 to sustain that rate. 

The primary bottleneck was in the 737 wing shop. Ortberg told analysts that some changes intended to speed up wing production had delivered smaller gains than Boeing expected. The company was adding capacity in parts of the shop and changing how work moved through it. Wing output had improved by October, but Boeing still couldn’t sustain the pace needed for 47 jets a month.

Boeing was also drawing down its fuselage stock, Reuters reported. Its Wichita plant produced new fuselages more slowly than final assembly required. Ortberg said Wichita would have to raise output to match the assembly rate as Boeing moved through that inventory.

Boeing is targeting 52 aircraft a month in the second half of 2027. Ortberg said the increase depends on certifying and bringing the Everett North Line into production, sustaining wing output and stabilising fuselage production in Wichita at higher rates.

Chief financial officer Jay Malave said the slower ramp would leave Boeing short of its 2026 target of 500 737 deliveries. Boeing expects deliveries of MAX 7 and MAX 10 aircraft built before certification to begin in early 2027. The FAA certified the MAX 7 in July and the MAX 10 in October.

Orders keep coming as output targets slip

Boeing ended September with a record $612 billion commercial aircraft backlog covering more than 6,300 jets. It booked 300 net orders in the third quarter, including orders from Turkish Airlines, Ethiopian Airlines and Lufthansa.

Demand also came from lessors. On 4 November, Boeing and Avolon confirmed the Dublin-based lessor had finalised an order for 140 737 MAX 10s. Boeing said lessors had placed firm orders for more than 230 MAX 10s in 2026.

787 output holds at eight aircraft a month

Ortberg said on the October call that 787 production was stable at eight aircraft a month. Boeing still expected to begin moving to 10 by the end of 2026, with engine deliveries dictating the pace. Seat certification had also contributed to uneven Dreamliner deliveries.

Boeing reported 161 commercial aircraft deliveries in the third quarter, including 124 737s and 22 787s. 

Boeing’s quarterly filing puts the next 787 rate increase in December. Further increases depend on expanding its Charleston factory and suppliers’ ability to support higher output.

]]> NTSB recovers Learjet 60 cockpit voice recorder after fatal Florida crash https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/ntsb-recovers-learjet-60-cockpit-voice-recorder-after-fatal-florida-crash/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 09:51:09 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56211 Investigators have recovered the cockpit voice recorder from the fatal Florida Learjet 60 crash, but don't yet know whether it contains any usable audio.

The post NTSB recovers Learjet 60 cockpit voice recorder after fatal Florida crash appeared first on AGN.

]]> The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) says it has recovered the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) from the Learjet 60 that crashed near Greenacres, Florida on 1 November, killing all nine people on board.

The recorder, commonly known as a ‘black box’, was discovered at the aircraft’s crash site near Greenacres in Palm Beach County. The NTSB confirmed the discovery in a social media post on 9 November.

It has now been taken to the agency’s Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington where experts are examining whether any usable audio can be recovered.

NTSB board member Tom Chapman has previously said it could contain “very important data”.

However, the NTSB has not yet confirmed whether it contains recordings of the flight.

What is the Learjet 60 cockpit voice recorder?

The aircraft black box is actually two devices: the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) and the flight data recorder (FDR). Larger airlines need to have both installed.

The Learjet was operated by Aurora Aviation, doing business as Upper Jets. It is a Part 135 operator, offering private jet flights on-demand.

Unlike commercial airlines, which operate under the FAA’s Part 121 rules, Part 135 operators are not always required to have both black boxes installed.

In a press conference on 2 November, NTSB board member Tom Chapman said the aircraft’s maintenance records suggested a CVR was installed. But he added: “What we don’t know is whether that recorder was still on board; sometimes these things change over time.

“We’re still seeking to determine whether there was a recorder, and then of course we’re very hopeful that we can recover it. It’s too early to know, but that’ll be very important data.”

Where is the cockpit voice recorder and what does it record?

The recorder has a “cockpit area microphone” which is usually located on the overhead instrument panel between the two pilots.

The NTSB explains that CVRs record radio transmissions and sounds in the cockpit, including the pilot’s voices and engine noises.

Automated radio weather briefings, communications with air traffic control and conversation between the pilots and ground or cabin crew are also recorded.

NTSB investigators have recovered the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) of the Learjet 60 that crashed on Nov. 1 near Greenacres, Florida. The CVR was located at the site of initial impact.​ The CVR is being evaluated in the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, D.C. The excavation work at the impact site has been completed.

— NTSB Newsroom (@NTSB_Newsroom) November 9, 2026

The NTSB says sounds of interest to investigators could include “engine noise, stall warnings, landing gear extension and retraction, and other clicks and pops.”

What could the Learjet’s black box reveal?

If usable audio is recovered, investigators may be able to reconstruct the crew’s actions, communications and awareness of developing problems.

The recording could also reveal warning sounds, engine noises and the timing of key events during the flight’s final moments.

Who will listen to the Learjet’s cockpit voice recorder?

A team of specialists will be set up to listen to the audio from the Learjet. This is called a CVR committee, and is usually made up of NTSB investigators, the FAA, the aircraft operator, the plane manufacturer, the engine manufacturer and the pilots union.

They will write a transcript of the CVR audio. This will then be used during the investigation into the fatal crash.

Will the audio be released?

A Congress ruling means the Safety Board can’t release any part of the CVR recording during the investigation.

However, parts of the audio can be released during any public hearing on the accident.

Harrowing audio of co-pilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras’ final radio calls were shared on social media last week.

The Learjet was travelling from Austin, Texas to the Bahamas when the crew reported encountering icing, turbulence and precipitation before the aircraft entered a rapid descent.

Nathalia could be heard reporting an outside air temperature of minus 47C and asked whether smoother conditions were available ahead as thunderstorms developed in the area.

After telling controllers they were encountering precipitation and requesting a climb to 37,000 feet, Nathalia told air traffic control: “We’re descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday – we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute.”

Seconds later, she is then heard saying: “Declaring emergency. We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute. We’re going to crash into the ground.”

Technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp and their two young children were among those who died.

Also onboard was the family’s nanny Anita Maria Cetina and two family friends Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr.

The plane’s captain, Jeff Gregory, 55, was also killed in the crash.

What else has been recovered from the Learjet crash site?

The NTSB revealed on 8 November that it has found components from both wings, both engines, the flight deck, vertical stabilizer, left elevator, aileron sections and multiple flap track assemblies.

It said it had also recovered the jet’s horizontal stabilizer – this had appeared to be missing in harrowing video footage of the crash that was shared on social media. 

Investigators had previously said portions of the jet’s left elevator were recovered between 1.3 and 3.8 miles from the impact site, suggesting the aircraft began breaking up before it crashed.

Parts of the wreckage have now been sent to NTSB laboratories in Washington for further examination.

]]> Airbus has claimed the world record for the longest flight by a commercial airliner, snatching the accolade from competitor Boeing after two decades.

The record was set by the Airbus A350-1000ULR, a specific variant of its flagship widebody aircraft developed for Qantas, to allow the Aussie airline to fly directly from Sydney to London and New York. To make such ultra-long flights possible, Airbus added an extra fuel tank, giving it a published range of around 10,000 nautical miles (nm).

But the world record-setting flight substantially exceeded this range, clocking in at over 12,500 nm and unseating Boeing’s 777-200LR ‘Worldliner’ as the longest flight by distance by a commercial airliner.

Airbus A350-1000ULR goes the long way round to set a new record

The record-breaking flight took place between 27 and 28 July this year, and saw the A350-1000ULR depart Melbourne and fly to Toulouse. A direct flight would cover around 9,100 nm – a long flight indeed, but not enough to break any records.

In order to go the distance, Airbus opted to travel the long way round, crossing two oceans in the process.

Leaving Melbourne on the afternoon of 27 July, the aircraft flew over Sydney and headed across the Pacific, crossing the international date line. It passed by Los Angeles and crossed the American continent before heading across its second ocean: the Atlantic.

From there, the flight headed south, crossing the UK and landing in Toulouse in the morning of 28 July. Airbus added that the 13 people onboard got to witness two sunrises and two sunsets during the journey.

The flight took a total of 24 hours and 24 minutes, and covered a distance of 12,503 nm. Airbus said the flight was part of the test campaign for the A350-1000ULR, which Qantas had requested be tested with a block time of 23 hours to simulate the very longest commercial operations it could face.

The official Guinness World Record for the longest flight by distance by a commercial airliner was announced on 9 November, and is based on aircraft data independently validated by the International Aeronautical Federation and Flightradar24.

Airbus A350 unseats the mighty Boeing 777

The previous record for the longest flight by distance by a commercial airliner was set 21 years ago, in November 2005.

Between 9 and 10 November 2005, Boeing flew its 777-200LR ‘Worldliner’ from Hong Kong to London. Like Airbus, it went the long way round the globe to give it the space for the demonstration. In all, the aircraft covered 11,664 NM nonstop before landing at Heathrow.

The flight took 22 hours and 42 minutes, and had a representative of the US National Aeronautic Association on board to monitor the attempt. Guinness representatives met the aircraft in London.

Boeing has previously held the record with the 747 and its 777-200ER. Airbus, too, had the crown for a while with its A340-200.

Previous world record-setting commercial flights

Why Airbus has made a plane that can fly for 24 hours

Located a long way from most of the populated world, Qantas is no stranger to long flights. But nonstop flights from Sydney to Europe and the East Coast of the US remained out of reach.

Qantas asked Airbus to develop a widebody aircraft that would be capable of routes like Sydney to London and New York.

Airbus answered that challenge with the A350-1000ULR. It had already developed a longer-range version of the smaller A350-900 for Singapore Airlines, which currently operates the world’s longest scheduled flights from Singapore to the New York area. It’s also stretched the range of its popular narrowbody A321neo into the XLR, and was well placed to do this again with its biggest aircraft.

The A350-1000ULR has an additional rear centre fuel tank which provides around 20,000 litres of extra capacity. Coupled with that is an upgraded maximum takeoff weight (MTOW), allowing it to carry the extra fuel. Airbus says this adds around 1,000 nm to the A350-1000’s range.

Alongside changes to the fuelling, the aircraft has a new lighter galley cooling system, which has saved around 300 kg of carried weight. Although this was developed for the ULR specifically, Airbus plans to make it standard across the A350 family.

The manufacturer thought of the humans on board too, with revised crew rest facilities for the pilots and cabin crew who will operate these mega flights. The passenger cabin is premium-heavy and includes a wellbeing zone for stretching and standing.

You can read more about how Airbus designed the A350ULR for Qantas in our deep dive here.

Qantas has ordered 12 A350-1000ULR for Project Sunrise, with the first delivery anticipated in the first half of 2027. The 20+ hour Sydney – London services are expected to begin later in the year, with New York to follow after.

An Indian Air Force (IAF) IL-76 MD heavy transport aircraft has landed at 13,629 feet at Nyoma airbase in eastern Ladakh, setting what the service says is a world altitude record for the aircraft type and demonstrating its ability to operate from a newly upgraded runway near the Chinese border.

The landing, carried out on Friday and announced by the IAF on Saturday, marks a significant development for India’s military airlift operations in the Himalayas. Nyoma lies approximately 25 kilometres from the Line of Actual Control (LAC) with China, where maintaining reliable supplies to troops deployed in difficult mountain terrain remains a major logistical challenge.

The IAF described the landing as “a remarkable demonstration of the aircraft’s enduring capability, backed by the exceptional skill, precision, and professionalism /f its crew”.

It called the achievement “a milestone that reinforces India’s strategic airlift capability”.

The flight also demonstrated the continuing relevance of the Russian-origin IL-76, an aircraft India began operating more than four decades ago.

From a basic airstrip to a strategic airbase

Nyoma’s transformation is central to the significance of the landing.

The airstrip was reactivated in September 2009 when an IAF Antonov An-32 transport aircraft landed there. Until recently, its facilities were better suited to smaller tactical transports and helicopters than large military freighters.

Following the military confrontation with China that began in 2020, India accelerated infrastructure development across Ladakh, including roads, bridges, tunnels and airfields.

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh laid the foundation stone for Nyoma’s redevelopment in September 2023.

The Border Roads Organisation subsequently constructed a 2.7-kilometre paved runway under a project costing approximately INR 2.18 billion (approximately $23.2 million). The development included aircraft parking areas, hangars and air traffic control facilities.

The upgraded airbase was inaugurated in November 2025 when then IAF chief Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh landed a C-130J Super Hercules there.

Its runway is designed to accommodate transport aircraft, helicopters and fighter operations, considerably expanding the military’s options in eastern Ladakh.

The arrival of the IL-76 provides evidence that the upgraded facilities can handle a substantially heavier aircraft than those previously operating from the old landing ground.

Why landing at 13,629 feet is difficult

High-altitude operations present challenges even for aircraft designed to use relatively austere airfields.

At Nyoma’s elevation, the air is considerably less dense than at sea level. Aircraft wings must move through the thinner air at a higher true airspeed to generate the lift needed for flight.

That means a transport aircraft can approach the runway at a higher ground speed for the same indicated airspeed, potentially increasing the distance required to stop.

Reduced air density also affects engine performance, particularly during take-off and climb.

Crews must account for aircraft weight, temperature, wind, runway conditions and the performance margins available at the airfield.

The IL-76’s high-mounted wings, four turbofan engines and robust undercarriage were designed to support military transport operations, including from relatively demanding runways.

However, the aircraft’s published payload capability cannot automatically be assumed at Nyoma. High elevation and operating conditions can impose substantial restrictions on the weight an aircraft can safely carry.

The IAF has not disclosed the aircraft’s landing weight or cargo load during the record flight.

An earlier milestone at Daulat Beg Oldie

India has previously demonstrated high-altitude airlift capability using the American-built C-130J Super Hercules.

On 20 August 2013, an IAF C-130J landed at Daulat Beg Oldie in northern Ladakh, at an elevation of approximately 16,614 feet.

The aircraft operated from a compacted-earth landing strip near the Karakoram Pass, demonstrating the ability to deliver personnel and supplies to one of India’s most remote military outposts.

The C-130J was developed for tactical airlift operations and is equipped to operate from short, relatively austere runways.

Its four turboprop engines, high-lift wing configuration and specialised landing gear make it particularly suitable for such missions.

The distinction between the two achievements is important.

The C-130J’s landing at Daulat Beg Oldie demonstrated its ability to operate at extreme altitudes using a relatively basic airstrip. The IL-76’s landing at Nyoma is a different achievement. Unlike the smaller C-130J, the IL-76 is a heavy transport aircraft designed to carry substantially larger loads, including armoured vehicles and bulky military equipment. Operating such a large aircraft at 13,629 feet presents its own challenges because the thin mountain air affects aircraft performance.

Why India’s ageing IL-76 still matters

Known as Gajraj (King Elephant) in IAF service, the IL-76 entered India’s transport fleet in 1985, initially equipping No. 44 Squadron.

India acquired 17 aircraft between 1985 and 1989, establishing a heavy-lift capability that had previously been beyond the reach of its smaller transport fleet.

The four-engine aircraft can carry approximately 40–45 tonnes under suitable operating conditions, including military vehicles, equipment and other bulky loads.

Its rear loading ramp allows heavy cargo to be moved into the aircraft without the specialised loading arrangements required by conventional passenger aircraft.

The IL-76 has been used to transport troops, armoured vehicles and equipment to forward military areas, including Ladakh. It has also supported humanitarian assistance, disaster relief and overseas operations.

The IAF subsequently acquired Boeing C-17 Globemaster III transports, which offer greater payload capacity and modern avionics.

Nevertheless, the IL-76 remains an important part of India’s available heavy-lift capacity, particularly when multiple aircraft are required to sustain large military deployments.

Its continued service also presents growing maintenance challenges.

The ageing airframes require structural inspections, engine maintenance and a reliable supply of replacement components. Obtaining Russian-origin spares has become more difficult, with supply problems aggravated by the war in Ukraine.

India has examined extending the technical life of some IL-76 aircraft while expanding domestic maintenance and repair capabilities. Russian technical support remains important, particularly for engines and specialised systems.

Proposals to keep the fleet operational into the 2030s or beyond depend on the condition of individual aircraft, the availability of spares and the viability of further upgrades. No confirmed fleet-wide service extension into the 2040s has been established.

India is also pursuing a Medium Transport Aircraft programme as part of its longer-term effort to modernise military airlift.
